Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 is out now, and the game features a lot of music from famous real-world artists. But Doja Cat is not among them. She's not happy about that, either. Doja Cat said online that she is "so f**kin bitter" about that. In follow-up posts, she told Rockstar to "eat my d**k." She said she loves GTA 6, and being left out of the game breaks her heart. Directing her posts at Rockstar in this way, with this language, is unlikely to win her any fans at the studio, so it would be surprising indeed if we see her music get added to the game at any point. https://twitter.com/DojaCat/status/2123433353521045682 Doja Cat's music is not on any of GTA 6's in-game radio stations, nor do any of her tunes feature on the 34-song GTA 6: The Album, which is out now. The album includes music from Travis Scott, Dua Lipa, Morgan Wallen, Young Thug, Cardi B, Keith Richards, Lana Del Rey, and more. The in-game radio stations, meanwhile, feature music from Tom Petty, George Strait, Glen Campbell, Bad Bunny, Drake, Lil Wayne, Slayer, Sepultura, System of a Down, and Tool, just to name few. For more, check out GameSpot’s GTA 6 review and our rundown of the five best things to do first. And if you're eager for news on GTA 7? Get comfortable, because Rockstar is not going to announce it anytime soon.

Kelly Clarkson's feud with the Art of Play store became one of the strangest stories of 2026, as who would've thought a story about a pop star trying to buy an animatronic bird would draw so much attention? While the beloved Clarkson might've taken some hits in the court of public opinion, it sounds like the artist on the other side of the drama saw a big boost in patronage.

Bliss Kolb, the artist responsible for the $15,000 bird that was eventually purchased by another celebrity, is getting a ton of orders after this brouhaha. The Wall Street Journal reported that he's seen over 100 requests for his work, and that he's trying to wind down the orders. With that remarked, he's happy for all the attention he received and mentioned Clarkson in his comment:.

I've wanted for people to know about my work for decades. I appreciate that she liked it. This is happening at a time that I'm trying to wind down commitments.

In a recent development, the 70-year-old artist who lives in Seattle isn't trying to ramp up the amount he's doing these days, but he is grateful for the spotlight on the work he's made throughout his life. Out of all the hatred that came from this drama, I'm happy to hear some positivity came out of it, too.

‘I Know This Sounds Dark.’ The Advice Kelly Clarkson Gives Contestants When The Voice Goes Live.

Recent findings suggest that for those needing a refresher, this all started when Kelly Clarkson wandered into a Brooklyn store and inquired about the price of an animatronic bird on the wall. There's a discrepancy about what happened afterward, but the pop star went online and alleged that a worker at the store implied she couldn't afford the asking price, apparently not knowing who she was.

The store, Art Of Play, told a different story. It was alleged that Clarkson was merely told the piece was one of a kind and not for sale. It became a big case of "he mentioned, she said," with people reviewing security camera footage and drawing their own conclusions about it. There was also the random reveal that the owner of the store is an acclaimed children's author, but that didn't really have anything to do with the story.

According to recent reports, kelly Clarkson has had a wild year, but there have been some upsides on the back half of 2026 for her. The Kelly Clarkson Show received some substantial honors following its end, and she seems to be largely at peace with leaving the daytime talk show circuit.

Who knows what's next for her as the holidays approach, but I can assume her kids won't be getting an expensive toy bird under the Christmas tree. However, based on the number of requests this artist is getting, it seems like it's perfectly possible that lots of folks would like to do something like that with his work.

‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Francis Lawrence on the Film’s Final Scene

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow.
  • Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment.
  • Industry observers note that just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the upcoming movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow. “All I need is a significant eagle back here,” the white-haired, smartly dressed director jokes.

Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment. He joined the franchise for its 2013 sequel, Catching Fire, and has directed only three non–Hunger Games movies in the decade-plus since. In that time, one could argue, the world has tilted further toward the oppressive future depicted in Collins’s novels—see, for instance, Donald Trump’s Hunger Games–esque Patriot Games. And while Lawrence isn’t naming names, he’s never lost sight of the movies’ larger political message. “I feel really lucky to be able to tell stories that matter, that are wrapped in these commercial packages,” he tells Vanity Fair. “So anytime one of these things comes around, I jump at it.”.

Industry observers note that just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the upcoming movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada. He plays the younger version of Woody Harrelson’s Haymitch Abernathy, a victor of the Hunger Games who later serves as a mentor to actor Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Making a reflective movie prompted director Lawrence to reflect on his own Hollywood trajectory. “The biggest difference is that I’m a lot more relaxed. I was nervous as hell on Catching Fire,” he notes. “It was my fourth movie. It was a movie I was inheriting. It was a massive movie, and it was a massive cast. So I was really intimidated. Now I have much more fun, I will say. I’m much more comfortable with actors, and the amount of actors, and with logistics. And there’s definitely a family that’s built into it, which is very important for me. There’s, what, 14 years of my life spent making these movies? So it has to be fun.”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: When did you become aware of Sunrise on the Reaping, and at what point did you and Suzanne Collins start discussing an adaptation?

Francis Lawrence: When we did the original series of movies, and we finished the last Mockingjay, she said she was done, and we thought that was it. Then she surprised me and Nina [Jacobson], the producer, with Ballad, however many years later. And she never tells us when she’s writing. Even when she has something to read, she never tells us what it’s about. She’s very superstitious about it all. So we got the call, which was very exciting. And she said, “Go to my agent’s house. There’s a manuscript. Let’s talk after you read it.”.

It has been revealed that I got to his house, sat in his backyard, and there was a manuscript and a copy of Catching Fire sitting on top of it with a few tabs in it. I opened to the tabs and saw that it had the portion where Katniss and Peeta were looking up the Haymitch Games, that sequence from the book. And I was like, Oh, she’s written the Haymitch story, which was very exciting. And that started the process that we always have, which is that I read the manuscript in one sitting, then read it a second time after having a conversation with Suzanne.

In a recent development, then I fly to Newly introduced York and meet her at Scholastic, and we sit up in a conference room for about a week going through the book, beat by beat, of what we think the movie is going to be. She and I lay it all out and chat, and she sits on her computer and writes a scriptment. Then that’s the thing that we turn over to the screenwriter.

How have you built that trust with the author of these books, having adapted them for more than a decade now?

In a recent development, that working process happened accidentally when I signed on to do Catching Fire. I had never done a sequel to someone else’s first movie before. And when Lionsgate and the first director, [Gary Ross], parted ways and I got the call, they didn’t have a script, but they had started the process of developing it before I was on board. And so I signed on based on the book and had planned a trip to Fresh York to meet with Suzanne.

According to recent reports, the script came on the day that I was traveling to Upcoming York. I read it, and it was not the movie that I wanted to make—because I loved the book, and it was not the book. Luckily, nobody else wanted to make that version of the movie either. Our meeting of me just picking her brain turned into, “This script doesn’t work. Let’s go through, page by page, and figure out the version of the movie we want to make.”.

That’s what really formed the bond—just working really, really closely with her. Spending 8 or 10 hours a day for a week or two in a conference room—me riffing on visual ideas and her talking about the story. We think the same way in terms of storytelling, structure, and she seemed to take to my visual ideas.

It has been revealed that there’s this weird dynamic that happens as we get closer to production. We’re usually developing the script pretty much within a week of shooting. But the production is also building. So you have thousands of people working, figuring out locations, traveling in different parts of the world. The stress levels are building.

Sources indicate that suzanne and I have related the relationship to almost like a mother-son relationship. It starts really lovely and creative, but then as we get closer and closer, it’s me being that late teen who’s ready to leave the home, like, Okay, enough’s enough. I’m going to go make the movie now. I have to say, I love the process. It’s not without its stress sometimes, but that’s part of the closeness of it all that I cherish.

How did this film’s futuristic-meets-1970s aesthetic come about?

It has been revealed that there was an element [of the story] that reminded me a bit of Alice in Wonderland, which then made me think of Jefferson Airplane, that song “White Rabbit,” which brought me to the ’60s and ’70s. Then you can look at characters certain ways. Like, Haymitch, you go, Okay, he’s from, like, young Bruce Springsteen, or Lenore Dove [played by Whitney Peak], like a young Stevie Nicks. And you get this hippie vibe. And the Capitol is that Warhol Studio 54 crowd, and Snow like a ’70s Yves Saint Laurent.

How do you go about casting a young Haymitch, finding an actor who can anchor the film like Jennifer Lawrence did in the original Hunger Games film?

Our casting director, Deb Zane, had met him, and I want to say before he did East of Eden. She had a lot of faith in him. We liked his self-tape a lot. But we knew that he was going to have to pull a lot off. He starts as a very optimistic, fun, playful, young guy in love, and in this movie has to turn into somebody that’s much closer to the Haymitch that we’re used to—cynical and a drunk. He’s going to have to go through a lot of emotional trauma, plus have that kind of mischievousness, irreverence, all these different elements that Woody [Harrelson] has naturally. And so we really put him through the ringer. We did a lot of tests, kept bringing him back, bringing him back, bringing him back. He and I were modulating how much Woody we feel in his performance.

It has been revealed that I want to make sure that everybody makes the role their own. That they find the spirit of the character and that it’s not trying to do an imitation of somebody. That’s true of Elle [Fanning] doing Effie, of Ralph [Fiennes] doing Snow, of Jesse [Plemons] doing Plutarch, Kieran [Culkin] as Caesar. Everybody has to figure out how to do it on their own. Then the weird thing is that Kelvin [Harrison Jr., who plays a young Beetee], has worked with Jeffrey [Wright] three times. So he’s fairly close with Jeffrey. When he got the role, he called and remarked, “You won’t believe this, but I’m actually playing the young version of you.” He could just conjure Jeffrey Wright. His voice, the speech patterns, the timbre of the sound of everything. It was pretty wild.

Were there storylines from the previous films that you felt you could plant Easter eggs for? I’m thinking specifically of the romantic chemistry between Effie and Haymitch.

There are certain Capitol characters where I give a lot of freedom for improvisation. Effie, Caesar, Drusilla [played by Glenn Close], there’s a lot of room for ad-libs. One of the elements that we definitely played with a bit came from an improvised moment in the [last] Mockingjay. We were shooting this scene in Atlanta outside of Snow’s mansion, which is one of the very last scenes of Katniss in the Capitol. She’s saying goodbye to Effie, and then Haymitch and Effie kiss.

Quite honestly, it was an idea because Woody just wanted to kiss Elizabeth Banks. But everybody thought it would be fun and that the fans would dig it, that Haymitch kissed her. Then it became this major thing of this hidden love that Haymitch and Effie have for one another. And Elle played into that a bit. So there’s, I would say, a hint of flirtation here between the two, less so on Haymitch’s side. His heart is obviously somewhere else in the story. But Elle definitely brought a bit of that to it. That was not scripted. That’s the fun of having great actors.

What was it like to reunite Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson from the original movies?

Recent findings suggest that jen and I have stayed close over the years. We’ve done four movies together. Josh, who basically has moved to Spain, I haven’t seen in a long time. Woody I see off and on and text every once in a while. But there was something really special about the three of them being back together.

According to recent reports, it’s also really, for the most part, the same crew from 2012, when we started making Catching Fire. It’s the same DP [Jo Willems], the same camera operator [David J. Thompson], the same AD [Christopher Surgent].

It has been revealed that [When] they got to the hotel, Jen and Josh were in the bar having a beer or something, and I was like, Okay, I won’t even shower. I won’t get out of my rain gear. I’ll just come in. The next thing you know, there were 40 of us who had been together since Catching Fire, the gang back together. It’s like a high school reunion or something, but in the best possible way.

According to recent reports, there’s a futility to what happens in this film, knowing where we end up in future movies. How do you handle that aspect of history being doomed to repeat itself?

Recent findings suggest that look, we’re doing a story where you know the lead character is going to make it out. It’s really about how he makes it out, and what he ends up being like at the end of it all. What I’m really pleased about is that the way Suzanne wrote the book, and the way I think we’ve ended the movie, there is a sense of hope that the tragedy is not for nothing. That was really notable to me. And one of the beautiful elements in the story, which comes a bit later, is this sense of, everybody has to find their voice. Everybody has to participate.

It really deals with this thing that I think is happening a lot today, where you find apathy: people not wanting to vote, feeling even if they do vote that it’s not going to matter. This idea that you have to be active, and you can’t expect immediate gratification—that everybody needs to stand up and it may take generations, but you still have to do it.

It has been revealed that outside of my screening on the Upper West Side, there was a group protesting Elon Musk and data centers because the documentary about him was playing at the theater. It was a reminder that there will always be something to rise up against, and always people who will be willing to do it.

Yeah, exactly. And ideally, at some point, if everybody stands up, something will change.

During the 13 years that you’ve worked in this universe, dystopia has felt more and more familiar. How have real-world events influenced your filmmaking?

It has been revealed that in the 56 years I’ve been alive, there’s never really been a time where I’ve felt like, Oh wow, everything is great. Nothing is wrong in the world. It always feels like there’s some dystopian sense about the world at any given time. And somehow Suzanne is always able to write these stories about it, which is what makes these movies feel timeless. A lot of people just see them as spectacles, but really they’re about our times very specifically. Almost in a subversive way, I feel like we’ve gotten to smuggle these ideas into these movies that a lot of people go see.

After years of waiting, GTA fans can finally play GTA 6, but some players are encountering a dreaded error code that makes the game crash or otherwise fail. People are reporting receiving the CE-108255-1 error code, which players might see when a game crashes mid-session or fails to load entirely. Crashing mid-game in GTA 6 would be particularly frustrating given how saves work. Sony's official word is that players can try updating their game to fix the glitch. If it's really that simple, that would be a welcome result. But people are saying that doesn't always work and are asking Rockstar to put out an official patch. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dJDf76QVv70 Reddit user Acrobatic-Promise458 encountered this issue and documented their experience. The person mentioned the game was working normally until they reached a certain point in the story, at which point the game crashes continually. They said Rockstar support directed them to Sony's own support team, but it was no use. People online (via Gizmodo) are theorizing that the crashing challenges with GTA 6 on PS5 might be due to the game's intense demands on the hardware, and it could be specifically tied to older PS5s. https://twitter.com/ghost_motley/status/2123465979791380670?s=20 Rockstar has yet to officially respond to these reports. Rockstar's official GTA 6 error troubleshooting page isn't much help, as it only links to the support sites for PlayStation and Xbox and offers no specific help. Players can submit a support ticket to Rockstar to get more help with this issue or others. These issues do not appear to be very widespread, but if you're experiencing the CE-108255-1 error on PS5, that's no consolation to you. GTA 6 has reportedly sold 25 million copies and earned more than $2 billion in revenue already, and those numbers are only expected to grow higher. Unlike the "Star Wars" saga, the "Hunger Games" franchise has defied the odds to deliver two stellar prequel films set before the events of the very first dystopian sci-fi action movie adapted from author Suzanne Collins' original books.

According to recent reports, after launching in 2012, "The Hunger Games" delivered a four-part major screen property telling the story of rebellious Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and an ensemble of revolutionaries attempting to topple the oppressive, wealthy government known as The Capitol. But the franchise has since returned with stories set decades in the past. This started with 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," which offered a rich portrait of a young Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth) acting as a mentor to a bold Hunger Games tribute named Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler).

Now, the story continues 40 years later, with the excellent "Sunrise on the Reaping" focusing on a young Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson in the previous movies, now played by Joseph Zada in the prequel) as he's forced into the 50th Hunger Games. This event marks the second Quarter Quell, which takes place 24 years before the first installment of the overall franchise.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" (watch the trailer) might be the most brutal, heartbreaking chapter of the "Hunger Games" franchise yet, if only because the fall of Haymitch Abernathy — from charming, kind-hearted District 12 citizen to hopeless, grizzled, bitter, and drunk Hunger Games victor turned tribute mentor — is incredibly heartbreaking.

In a recent development, what happened to Haymitch after the 50th Hunger Games that sent him on a downward spiral? Join us as we explain the ending of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" to break it all down.

Before we explain the ending of "Sunrise on the Reaping," we need to set the stage a bit, so you know how and why Haymitch ends up where he does by the end of the movie.

Haymitch didn't have rebellion burning in his heart as the 50th Hunger Games were beginning, though his girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) put the spark of revolution in his mind, longing for a day when the sun would not rise on another reaping, overshadowing Haymitch's birthday. But Haymitch took it all in stride, even going out of his way to get a little bag of gumdrops for Lenore.

Unfortunately, Haymitch ends up in the 50th Hunger Games while trying to break up an altercation between Lenore and the Capitol police after she tries to let a grieving mother embrace her son, who has just been shot following an attempted escape from his obligation as one of the four District 12 tributes. District 12 tribute escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close), a cruel Capitol citizen, then punishes Haymitch by forcing him to be the replacement tribute, with a little behind-the-scenes editing help from Hunger Games broadcast producer Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons, playing a younger version of the character portrayed by the late Philip Seymour Hoffman in the original franchise).

It has been revealed that if that wasn't enough to light the spark of rebellion in Haymitch's heart, the events of the 50th Hunger Games welcome parade for the tributes certainly did the trick. After Capitol citizens throw colorful smoke flares into the Capitol arena where the parade is held, the horses pulling tributes in chariots get startled, creating a chaotic scene that results in the death of Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), a younger girl who admires Haymitch and was drawn as one of his three other fellow tributes.

After the death of Louella, Haymitch wants nothing more than to lash out at the Capitol, and he begins doing so by walking up to President Snow's (Ralph Fiennes) balcony in the parade arena and mockingly applauding him for directly bringing about the death and destruction laying in front of him.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Haymitch is also joined in the 50th Hunger Games by fellow District 12 tributes Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), a somewhat snobby and sassy 16-year-old girl who has a reputation for being a bit mean. But once forced into the Hunger Games, she softens and allies with Haymitch and the rest of the District 12 tributes. That includes Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), who comes from a family known as the "Booker Boys," because their family calculates odds and takes bets on the Hunger Games, which many view as a cruel practice. And despite the death of Louella, a Capitol-controlled lookalike replacement girl (Iona Bell) is forced to take her place, and the District 12 tributes take her under their protection.

Industry observers note that wyatt is killed almost as soon as the Hunger Games begin, when the tributes make a wild dash for weapons. But Haymitch, fake-Louella, and Maysilee make it out alive, though the former has chosen to disassociate himself from the rest of the group, having been told directly by President Snow that he will not make it out of the Hunger Games alive, as penance for his mocking defiance at the parade. Haymitch doesn't want anyone else to suffer for his defiance. But little does Snow know that Plutarch Heavensbee, with the help of several other Hunger Games mentors and tributes, are using Haymitch as a vessel for a rebellion meant to stop the games once and for all.

In a recent development, in the games, Haymitch works with a clever tribute named Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV), who is mentored by his father Beetee (the tech-wise character played by Jeffrey Wright in the original films, now played by Kelvin Harrison Jr.). They've concocted a initiative to break the Hunger Games by blowing up the water tank that supplies the entire arena, flooding the computer systems and cutting off power to the entire operation. Haymitch succeeds initially, but the power is repaired quickly, Ampert is killed by woodland creatures swarming and gnawing his body to death, and as retaliation for the attack on the arena, Snow orders that the arena's volcano be activated.

Haymitch survives the eruption, and the deadly fire that engulfs the mountainous woods of the arena, but most of the surviving tributes do not (including fake-Louella, who died earlier by way of a poison pollen), leaving just five of them: Maysilee, a young girl named Wellie (Rada Rae), and two of the deadliest career tributes, Silka and Panache (Laura Marcus and Jhaleil Swaby).

After a series of attacks, both by deadly birds and Silka and Panache, all of the other tributes have died, including Maysilee, but not before they promise each other to be the worst Hunger Games victor ever, should they emerge victorious. Haymitch is crowned as the victor of the Hunger Games, and he intends to stay true to his promise. But his battle is only just beginning, and it's about to get much worse.

According to recent reports, haymitch might have won the Hunger Games, but all of his actions in the arena are painted in a completely different light. His attack on the arena itself is not televised, and when he's presented to the Capitol as the winner in the recap hosted by Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin), he's painted as a traitor and a coward, one who promised to help his fellow tributes against the careers but abandoned them as soon as the games started. Even the final kill of Silka, which happens after her thrown axe is deflected back at her by a shield protecting the power plant that gives energy to the arena, is mocked, as Haymitch couldn't even deliver the final blow himself to declare victory.

Things don't get better when he returns home, either. As soon as he arrives back in District 12, his mother and brother are killed in a house fire, clearly orchestrated by President Snow. But the final crushing blow comes when he reunites with Lenore. As they embrace, she eats what appears to be the gumdrops that he told his brother to give to Lenore before he left for the Hunger Games. But those aren't the same gumdrops. They're poisoned, courtesy of Snow, and Lenore dies in Haymitch's arms.

All of this pushes Haymitch to the brink, and he begins to drink heavily and isolate himself from the rest of District 12, even shunning the friendly Everdeen family, despite their efforts to help him work through the pain. He stays true to his word by becoming the worst Hunger Games victor, letting his tributes fail for years, refusing to participate in this barbaric entertainment. But there might yet be hope for Haymitch.

Recent findings suggest that why did President Snow let Haymitch live after defying the Capitol so clearly? In addition to being the victor of the Hunger Games, making it difficult for him to merely dispatch with him in the arena, Plutarch Heavensbee convinced Snow to reconsider killing Haymitch after the games were over. Knowing that their stunt to end the games didn't work, and the public was unable to see the tributes working together and sparking the rebellion in the districts needed to overthrow the Capitol, Heavensbee is pulling a move that feels reminiscent of Albus Dumbledore using Harry Potter to draw out Voldemort.

According to recent reports, plutarch is the one orchestrating the presentation of the Hunger Games to the public, and he knows what they need to see in order to sew a revolution properly. He's willing to turn Haymitch into an outcast and upend his life if it means there's even the smallest possibility that his defiance will eventually grow into the rebellion they need. He knows the continuation of the games will continue to create resentment, and they just need to wait for the right spark to emerge that will set fire to the hearts of every district in Panem. While it might feel like they've failed, this is still a small success that will lead to a future generation following in their footsteps.

We already know how that story turns out, and "Sunrise on the Reaping" ends with Woody Harrelson returning as Haymitch Abernathy, admiring a memorial that now lies where the reaping once took place in District 12. He's joined by Katniss and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), who wish him a happy birthday, allowing Haymitch to fulfill Lenore's dreams of keeping the sun from rising on another reaping. Haymitch paid dearly for decades, but the Hunger Games are finally over.

GTA 6 is an enormous hit--it's the biggest gaming release ever. Take-Two just confirmed that GTA 6 reach 32.5 million copies sold before release, with revenue reaching $3.79 billion through the end of the first day on sale on November 19. This makes it the biggest entertainment release--for any medium--in history, Take-Two remarked. For comparison, 2013's GTA 5 hit $800 million in revenue in its first 24 hours and $1 billion after its first three days, so GTA 6 is pacing well ahead of those numbers. GTA 5 debuted at $60, compared to $80 for the cheapest version of GTA 6. For comparison, the all-time highest-grossing movie ever is Avengers: Endgame, which made $2.94 billion during its entire run. Sensor Tower had been sharing unofficial sales data for GTA 6 for a long time already, but Take-Two's sales numbers are even higher than the 25 million sales that Sensor Tower reported at launch. GTA 6 is only going to get bigger when it comes to sales as more and more people buy the game. Additionally, GTA 6 is expected to come to PC in 2027, which will be another selling cycle for the game. Beyond this, GTA 6 is expected to add an online mode in 2027 that will no doubt feature microtransactions and other ways for Rockstar to make money off the fanbase. It's been well established that Selena Gomez, Martin Short and Steve Martin know how to get into hilarious trouble on Only Murders in the Building, which you can stream with a Hulu subscription. However, the members of the unexpected trio know how to do that in real life too. Need an example? Look no further than the time Martin Short accidentally cut Gomez's wedding cake, and her hilarious reaction to it.

Earlier this year, Short had nothing but wonderful things to say about Selena Gomez and Benny Blanco's wedding. However, the reception featured some unexpected chaos. The comedy legend admitted he cut into the bride and groom’s cake, not realizing it was not for the guests until people started shouting at him. And it didn’t help that it was just before the newlyweds were supposed to cut into it themselves. While appearing on Jimmy Kimmel Live! with Short, Gomez shared her take on the whole situation and was a very good sport:.

But I love the teeth marks of the fork, where he tried to save it. Really nicely done.

I do love that Short tried his hardest to cover it up, but I can’t say I blame him for cutting into the cake. He revealed that there were different sections at the reception with couches and groups of people, and he simply thought there was a cake in each section.

I also love that Gomez is not even upset about it and is more impressed with the fact that her co-star tried to save it. Weddings can be stressful, even after the fact, but I’m glad to know that they knew how to roll with the punches, even when Short didn’t want the bride to know, as she explained:.

Industry observers note that so, he apparently insisted, no one tell me, no one tell me, no one tell me. And they managed to put it together, and I didn’t care, I was there, but I didn’t know what happened. And then all the sudden, somebody comes up to me and goes, ‘Marty cut your cake.’ I was like, ‘Oh!’ So, I run, I think he looks like a little dog with his tail between his legs, and I go, ‘I heard you ate my cake!’.

Considering how close Gomez and Short have become over the years, I love that there were no hard feelings over the accidental cake cutting. It also further proves why they’re bestie goals. Even now, she laughed the entire time retelling the story, which Short claims he is “blameless” in.

While this may have come as a shock at first, ultimately the mistake from Short made the night even better. As Gomez recalled, she's actually grateful it happened, and it helped make the whole event even more unforgettable:.

We will always have that memory together, and honestly, I’ll never forget it, and I’m grateful you tried to eat my cake.

According to recent reports, the friendship between Short, Martin, and Gomez is definitely the best thing to come out of Only Murders in the Building. Of course, Short and Martin have long been friends, but I definitely feel like Gomez was the missing piece. Now, I hope there are many more funny stories like this to come.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some big numbers that speak to the pent-up demand.
  • Sources indicate that rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some massive numbers that speak to the pent-up demand.
  • For starters, the internet service provider Comcast unveiled that November 18--the final day of preloading--was the busiest day in the tech giant's history in terms of demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some big numbers that speak to the pent-up demand. GTA 6 sold more than 30 million copies and hit almost $4 billion on day one, but that's just the start of understanding the impact of the game's release. For starters, the internet service provider Comcast announced that November 18--the final day of preloading--was the busiest day in the company's history in terms of demand. Peak traffic was 31% higher than an average day and a full 9.6% higher that the previous biggest day ever for traffic to Comcast's network. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ble-JJxBBGA GTA 6 also now holds five of the top 10 busiest days of Comcast's network of all time. Going further, Comcast remarked around 24% of all internet traffic on Comcast's network was people downloading or playing GTA 6 on November 18 (no doubt thanks to the New Zealand trick). Additionally, traffic to Twitch on Comcast's network was up by almost 50% and "is still increasing," Comcast said. A spokesperson for Comcast further contextualized the traffic data, telling GameSpot that between when preloading began on November 10 and through November 18, PlayStation and Xbox traffic pushed enough data on the network for one million homes to stream The Odyssey in 4K repeatedly for two days straight. Comcast was among the internet service providers that offered free speed boosts to subscribers to help them download GTA 6 faster. Additionally, Mat Piscatella of Circana shared data that speaks to the enormity of GTA 6's launch on PlayStation and Xbox. For active accounts November 19 in the US, 61% of PS5 accounts "engaged with" GTA 6. On Xbox, 56% of Xbox players globally did. PS5 players averaged 513 minutes of play for GTA 6 on November 19, compared to 494 on Xbox. These daily active user and minutes played figures are "absolutely bonkers," Piscatella said. GTA 6 was No. 1 on November 19, pushing Fortnite down to No. 2 based on these engagement metrics, Circana said. For more, check out GameSpot’s GTA 6 review and our rundown of the five best things to do first. And if you’re eager for news on GTA 7? Get comfortable, because Rockstar is not going to announce it anytime soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.

Industry observers note that this year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. But you’re probably more likely to associate Hasan’s name with what other people have had to say about him—from Fox News commentators to more established members of the Democratic Party.

In a recent development, hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s said things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel. He claims he’s often taken out of context, and that his audience knows what he really means—and where he stands. In his mind, he’s a leftist provocateur, maybe, but one who understands the importance of working-class values and electoral strategy.

In a recent development, while Hasan has walked back some of his more inflammatory language, his rhetoric raises the question: Is he a liability to the cause he champions? Or is he successfully reaching the critical audience—namely, young men—that helped elect the wave of progressives poised to take office in January?

Recent findings suggest that with 2028 on the horizon, I wanted to know how Hasan thinks about his growing platform, and if he sees his role shifting in the media landscape. What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?

We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.

Mark Guiducci: Hasan Piker, welcome to Fair Game.

Hasan Piker: Very excited to be here.

You reach tens of thousands of people at a time on average, and it’s all in the channel that you control. I’m curious, what are you doing here with me today? Why are you showing up for a show with a legacy media publication? What’s in it for you?

They talk about me a lot. And also I’ve never been invited on any of these outlets as a pundit either, which is also strange because, as you also pointed to, I don’t just operate as a campaignster. I have. Gavin, Gavin, come on the show. I am a taxpaying California resident. I’m one of your constituents. You want to be president in 2028, you’re gonna have to be able to talk to people like myself.

It has been revealed that but, you know, a lot of people would say that impeachment would be a distraction. So I guess what I’m saying is, if you had to choose three agenda items that the Democrats are agreeing on and they’re going forward with—you already said subpoenas and investigations.

I’m perfectly fine with that. I’ve joked about that for years ’cause he’s so invested. He’s such a petty despot and so narcissistic that—.

I would say this is more performative.

I’m much more civil here. I’m not going to talk in the same way that I do on my broadcast. But here’s the thing, I can’t be fake on my broadcast. And I’m not even saying I’m being fake here. I’m just being nice.

But what I will say is this: A lot of people don’t realize that this is an interactive medium. Most people think, when they see a clip, especially if it’s chopped a certain way—.

According to recent reports, yes. Most people think this is my preproduced, prescripted statement ’cause that’s all they’ve seen from the Jake Tappers of the world. They don’t realize that I am offering extemporaneous commentary on a breaking news story in real time, without a production team, while simultaneously—.

No. While simultaneously duking it out with anonymous accounts. What is the one thing that everybody hates on Twitter and everywhere else on the internet?

The comment section. My entire platform revolves around yelling at the comment section, and the comment section is yelling back at me.

We’ve got to get you a practice.

In a recent development, but that is like, I’m in the zone. That’s when I’m in the pocket. I love being in that space.

You’ve been outspoken about distinguishing criticism of Israel from antisemitism, but do you think that there are moments when legitimate anger at Israel can create an environment in which antisemitism becomes acceptable, even among people who would never consider themselves antisemitic?

And what responsibility do you think you have, given the size of your audience and your influence with it, to call that out when it happens?

I do call it out when it happens, and it happens quite frequently. It’s not a secret that antisemitism has exploded in the Western world, especially after October 7. And that is why I take special care and consideration when talking about this issue in particular. Whenever I talk about Israel, there’s always going to be some people who will be like, “Well, you know how the Jews are.” And I will always take the time out to explain to my audience, and to whoever’s saying an offensive statement or an antisemitic statement, why they’re wrong. And I think it’s important to do that, not because—it’s not like the canary mission of the ADL is gonna be like, “This guy that we have presented to you as a prominent critic of Israel, that we’re desperately trying to paint as an antisemite, has actually spent thousands of hours combating antisemitism and will continue to do so because he’s an antifascist.” They don’t want to present the complexity of that argument because, let’s be real, it’s pretty tough trying to defend Israel. It’s not an easy endeavor.

Can you think of a time when you contributed to that problem, not intentionally, but maybe through something you said and the way your audience responded?

It has been revealed that no, because every clip that people post, or every moment that people have posted to point to this suspected antisemitism that I harbor, oftentimes is sandwiched between a comment that I have made leading up to it that completely destroys the narrative. The example I will present to you is the famous moment where I got disavowed by the entire Democratic Party. I noted something that I have said as an anti-Zionist for the last decade and will continue to say because it’s the truth: that Jews are not monolithic and that Israel should not be the responsibility of the entire Jewish population, and that anti-Zionism is not antisemitism; however, that forced conflation of Jews in Israel is increasing antisemitism. And they chopped it up and packaged it and turned it into this major media moment.

According to recent reports, so speaking of misinterpretations, you recently filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, although you’ve noted you were very deliberately anti-litigation for a long time before that. So what changed? Why this suit? And who else are you planning to sue?

So what changed is the heinous nature of this defamation. It was definitely a bridge too far. I feel like there is a boundary that was crossed that I could no longer abide by. And there’s a level of defamation and slander that takes place in the political conversation, but what Scott Jennings did was so disgusting and so malicious that I had to demand a retraction. Snopes did an article immediately because it was so heinous. He claimed that I was on video advocating to lynch Black voters. I’ve spent my entire life fighting against white supremacy, and the fact that they maliciously edited this video to make it seem like I was in favor of something that I’ve always been in opposition to, something so heinous, a hate crime, was outright unacceptable. So I wish that it didn’t have to get to litigation, but for some strange reason, they decided not to respond to our request for a retraction and now we’re here.

Who else are you planning to sue?

I mean, there are a lot of people who have engaged in that exact same kind of defamation and slander. So whoever has participated in it should probably be on the lookout.

Okay. In the national chapter of the DSA, there are some pretty extreme platform positions that—I saw Mamdani answer these questions on Fox News the other night. I’m sure you did too.

And I'm actually just curious where you stand on some of them.

So here’s the thing with the platform in its entirety. I think the format itself doesn’t actually do justice to the program, to describe the program, and it’s almost impossible to explain it as an elected representative or a mayor in a hostile or contentious media environment, if you’re on Fox News or whatever. The issue, I think, with the program is, there are certain elements of it that I don’t agree with fundamentally, but it’s a democratically organized, democratically voted-on program that DSA members voted for. And the way I see it is, these are very, very long-term goals, and I think this is not talked about in mainstream media at all. It is a platform, but it’s more so a North Star that we are working toward. Designing society in a way that yields egalitarian outcomes. That we do away with certain systems of cruelty is an honorable goal, is a just goal, even if I don’t fully agree with some elements of it.

In a recent development, I’m not a prison abolitionist; I’m not a police abolitionist. The reason why I don’t believe in that concept is because I think that these are necessary functions that must exist, but also must serve the people. Right now it doesn’t. It serves capital and that needs to change, that needs to be retooled. However, I also recognize that the current system that exists is far more ruthless, far more insane, even if we’ve normalized it, than even police abolition is. So from my perspective, if we look at where we’re at, the carceral state that exists, where America has 25% of the entire planet’s prisoner population despite only making up 4% of the overall population, and the recidivism rates that we have in this country, and the fact that we even have a private prison system in this country—that’s insane. That is insane by global standards. So it’s tough for me to sit here and say I oppose the DSA platform and program when I understand what they are trying to communicate.

And also, I think what is the regular order of business right now is far more insane than even prison abolition. Even though prison abolition is far-fetched and I don’t agree with it, I think the best possible way to go about it would be to have an electoral program, the perceivable, the permissible, the possible, and then the long-term goals, the long-term agenda, ’cause it’s not going to be easy to run and try to win on a platform that is not only idealistic, but also does not reflect the current societal understandings of concepts. Because most people think cops are awesome, they can do no wrong, they’re heroes, they’re constantly fighting crime, and they’re stopping rapes from happening, and they’re diving in front of bullets, but that’s not the case. I wish that was the case, but that’s not the case. But people overall [have] a very positive attitude about policing as an institution.

In a recent development, but there’s also quick and quippy ways to respond fast. I just told you I’m a law-and-order Democrat, right?

Immediately that signals something. Another thing that I always say about policing is, I want police to do their jobs. I think that, by and large, they have a profoundly important task that they have to accomplish. Their presence is supposed to invoke law and order. Their presence sometimes invokes lawlessness and disorder. That’s unacceptable. They’re very well paid. They have the best unions. Do your jobs better. That’s my attitude on policing. So it’s antagonistic, but it’s also a demand that I’m making from this institution that I truly do believe is important for society to function. That’s one way to tackle this issue in a way that Americans understand. I like to call it chudifying your commentary. Zohran does a very good job of libifying his commentary. He’s very liberal-appealing. I like to do the opposite. I like to chudify it. I appeal to the chuds. I speak from that tone and that language when I advocate for certain things.

Recent findings suggest that yeah, edgelord vernacular, sure. But it’s kind of like, whether we’re talking about abortions or whether we’re talking about transgender bills, like anti-trans bills, I’m like, I don’t want the fucking government getting involved in these affairs. What do you want? You want some creepy pervert to do penis inspection day at your high school? What are you, a pervert? Are you a pedophile? I want small government when it comes to this kind of stuff. And that is a way to argue from a perspective that I think right-wingers can understand.

In a recent development, switching gears, we talked a little bit about suits for a second, but I want to talk about style more largely. So at the RNC’s midterm convention in September, there was a 25-foot selfie of you in underwear displayed on the jumbotron. How do you think about that?

It’s a strange thing because I wish I was as in shape right now as I was, because that was peak.

Thank you. But also at the same time, I’m like, Oh, I wish I looked like that right now.

Sources indicate that why do you think they’re so obsessed with your looks? What is going on there? How is that helpful to them actually?

Industry observers note that it’s not. I think about that quite a bit. I think…they’re gay.

That’s it. I think they’re in the closet. There are a lot of Republican operatives that are just either gay or in the closet and haven’t been able to figure out how to communicate their desires. So they were just frustrated and confused. But there’s no other reason to have this pathological, this psychosexual, obsession where you’re like, “My opponent, this political opponent, is a dangerous guy. He’s a radical communist, Islamist, jihadist.”.

According to recent reports, “And he’s also sexy. Look at him shirtless. Look at him shirtless.” Because I thought these guys were peak masculinity. I thought that’s what they were about. The Joe Rogan Experience, you know, Brazilian jiujitsu, and working out was supposed to be the thing in the right.

There’s nothing unmasculine about being gay.

I’m kidding. That’s not how they think of it. I know.

And not only that, but also, ultimately, why are they showing a shirtless photo of me where I look jacked?

Recent findings suggest that yeah. Okay. But it’s not just the GOP. Almost any coverage of you, including now this, includes a reference to your appearance. And I’m sorry we’re doing this right now.

Do you like it in some regard, or does it bother you?

Sources indicate that it’s attention. I like it. In the past, when people would approach me and be like, “Why is The Newly introduced York Times only talking about how you look and not talking about your ideas?” I was like, “Look, that is terrorism insurance.” If I’m getting into these legacy publishers and not being called a terrorist and instead being called a hot guy, I’ll take it.

Okay. Okay. One last question about your looks. If Calvin Klein calls tomorrow and wants you to do the Houston Street billboard, are you doing it?

It has been revealed that I would need to immediately get on a steroid regimen. I would need to look like Kumail Nanjiani before.

Recent findings suggest that I mean, yeah, I would do it. Why wouldn’t I do it?

Okay. I wonder, with your audience, because there are a bunch of young guys looking up to a guy who’s maybe slightly older than them, looks like they might want to look, is that homoerotic at all?

But I do have a fairly queer community as well. We do a census. We do a yearly census. Fourteen percent of my audience is trans, which is obviously much higher than the American population.

What are some other demos that would be interesting that we wouldn’t expect?

Well, the classic ones are obviously—it’s like 60% white men under the age of 35.

You perform best with all the people that Vanity Fair performs worst [with].

I think a lot of mainstream outlets are really bad at captivating the attention of young men in particular. That’s probably part of the reason why people are always fascinated with this group. They’re trying to understand it.

Recent findings suggest that what about you captured them? How did you do it?

I was a young man at some point, and I also have the same interests, and I think that’s part of it. And I also speak—going back to the crude, the language that I deploy, the vulgar language that I deploy, it’s like I speak like a normal person. I speak and get angry in the same exact ways that normal people do.

According to recent reports, all right. Hasan, what’s your attitude toward money? How do you think about money?

Industry observers note that for me personally, it has a corrosive influence, I think. It has the capacity to make you unbelievably out of touch. It’s something that I think about quite a bit in my own personal experience. I was a very stubborn person with air travel. Even when I had a little bit of additional income, I refused to pay the extra for the economy-plus seats.

It has been revealed that I’m a major dude. I’m 6’4”, I can’t fit in the seats, and I would still. It’s a point of pride. Until one day I was put in a business class seat for some kind of business travel. And at that point I had enough money to purchase business class seats on my own, and I was like, I’m never looking back.

According to recent reports, you were ruined. You were ruined.

Industry observers note that it ruined me. It completely ruined me. So now—.

Tina Brown claims that the private plane ruins people, that when you see how that works, it’s over. Hook, line, sinker, people are done.

That corruption is almost—she doesn't say this, but I’m interpreting that it’s almost inevitable after that.

In a recent development, yes. I think that every instance of financial stability or financial freedom that I’ve gained has made me more out of step with the struggles that I used to experience and the struggle that everyday people experience. And I think you have to always be in touch. Especially in my line of work, you have to understand where people are. On the other hand, though, it is editorial freedom, because I have been able to maintain complete editorial control, complete editorial freedom, because I am completely unbought, completely unbossed, completely unshackled. There have been numerous instances where I’ve obviously had contracts with Amazon and stuff like that because I know I need to play ball also to make sure that I am a reliable team player so they don’t deplatform me. However, there have been so many instances where people have come to me with tremendous sponsorship opportunities.

According to recent reports, polymarket is one that I talk about all the time. [For] 2024 election night, their opening salvo was a million dollars just to have their ticker on the side. I stated, of course, no, because I feel like it’s deeply unethical to be sponsored by a gambling organization, a prediction market, while, you know, you’re engaging in news commentary. But I know that if I did not have that economic freedom, that financial freedom, I would’ve probably had to think about whether or not I’d make this ethical compromise.

So Calvin Klein would be an exception.

Industry observers note that calvin Klein’s fine. I mean, I take sponsorships every now and then, like gaming companies and stuff like that. If Rockstar came to me and were like, “Grand Theft Auto VI is coming out. We want to sponsor a stream,” I would fucking love that.

Sources indicate that some people have a number that’s like their retirement number, at which point that’s all the money they need. They close up shop and call it a day. I wonder if you have a number after which you think it would be unethical to accumulate any more. What is the maximum amount of net worth or income that you could generate after which you would feel it’s morally reprehensible?

Recent findings suggest that great question. I have no idea. I’ve never thought about it like that because there’s no world in which I will reach that number. But all the revenue that I generate goes immediately back into this broader project. It allows me to be able to travel around the country. It allows me to be able to hire people on a moment’s notice if necessary. So that’s the way I see it. I don’t have an unethical number, but I think to each their own, because I don’t want people to hear me say this and then be like, “Well, you know, you’ve collaborated with Saikat Chakrabarti. He’s a centimillionaire. You’ve talked to Tom Steyer. He’s a billionaire.” I care more about what people’s actual advocacy is and if they’re real about it or not. And I think how much they pay into certain things can show that, for sure. But anything past the point of having—not your net worth, right, but anything past the point of just having $10 million, I feel like is insane. It’s like, What are you doing? Does that make sense?

Because you said you differentiate with net worth.

I differentiate it with net worth because everyone will say, “Oh, well, I have assets. I have stocks,” or whatever. But in general, if you have—.

In a recent development, the capacity to deploy—I feel like even $10 million is too much. If you have the capacity to deploy a million dollars into something, you’re done, you’re set. I think everything past that point is outright ridiculous.

All right. I want to look ahead to the future because 2028 is not far away, and I think all signs would show that you’re going to be a character in that cycle. So here’s the inevitable 2028 question: Do you think the public has met the 2028 candidate that you’ll champion yet, or do you think that person is still waiting in the wings somewhere?

I mean, the top answer, obviously, since we’re doing this will-they-won’t-they thing, is AOC. Right? She is the one figure, I think, on the left that has the capacity to unite the base, and she’s competent, she’s charismatic, incredible progressive track record as a legislator, and—.

Who is moving more to the center.

Well, I think all that stuff is—it’s pragmatism. I don’t think that means that she is going to come out and be like, “I am no longer in favor of the same comprehensive policy agenda that I’ve sought to advance my whole life.”.

But it might mean that she wants to unite the base.

Yeah. But I don’t think you necessarily have to do compromise on the legislative front to unite the base. If I was being fully transparent, fully honest, or maybe a little harsh, my criticisms around AOC would probably be that she’s not aggressive enough and that at times she’s come across as perhaps a little too liberal, too woke, on social problems in a way that is not appealing to broad subsets of the base.

Industry observers note that okay. Say AOC runs but loses the primary, and you’re dealing with Josh Shapiro or Gavin Newsom or insert centrist Democrat here.

According to recent reports, what do you proposal to do? Do you urge your audience to get behind them?

In a recent development, I don’t know. I don’t know what I would do at that point. I haven’t even thought about it because I don’t think I need to think about it.

I don’t think it’s even going to be a problem.

So, I guess AOC or not, how do you want to be involved in the 2028 election?

I’m gonna do what I did in the primaries and the midterm broadly, and hopefully we’ll have a slate of hundreds of democratic socialists that will be running in every district that will be bold, that will excite the base, and that will chart a different path forward for the Democratic Party by force.

Do you think that—we’ve talked a little bit about this toxicity of the brand of Hasan Piker, which has been burnished by the right and by some on the left.

According to recent reports, do you think about trying to clean that up, as it were, so that you could be more helpful to whoever that progressive candidate is? Or is it more useful for you to be ethically pure, I guess, in your estimation and stay as the stick in the mud on the far left?

Sources indicate that look, I got to the point I got to by being honest and sometimes being hardheaded, being stubborn, but always saying the truth. And that policy’s not going to change. So I say, if this is considered too toxic for politicians to take advantage of this platform, then they’ll lose. Because my goal is not to change myself. My goal is to change politics. I want American politics to be more responsive, not only to our demands, but also reflective of our anger as well. I truly believe that we are in the moral majority. People who look at the current system and say, “This is not helping,” people who look at their insurance premiums going up and say, “We need to change this,” that is a morally righteous fury that people feel, and there is a great deal of time and effort spent on mainstream outlets, legacy publishers in the media broadly, to try to quiet that frustration. I believe that I have a more honest approach to the matter, and that is precisely the reason why my audience continues to grow as their audience continues to age out or diminish.

It has been revealed that I want to end on a slightly different note. I want to do a lightning round with you. I’m gonna say a series of names and I just want you to give me word association, the first thing that comes to your mind—just don’t say their job. It’s too boring.

Industry observers note that oh, there’s so many directions I can go with this. Do I joke? Do I fib? Do I say what I honestly think?

You just gave me a whole speech about being honest.

Well, on my broadcast, I joke and I call him the “sex panther” because he’s so uncharismatic, but I joke and say, “Oh my God, he’s so hot. He’s so charismatic every time he comes out and delivers this speech, finger-wagging speech.” But the serious answer, the one-word serious answer, would be corrupt.

Recent findings suggest that shit. Damn it. That works for Kim too.

I thought you were gonna say the same thing.

Sources indicate that I don’t want to repeat. I don’t want to repeat. Kim Kardashian, white feminist.

Recent findings suggest that oh damn. I used “manlet” for Stephen Miller. Can I use multiple words for Nick Fuentes?

Yeah, yeah. Please give me money. Fund the DSA.

Ooh, a lot of deployment of the word “manlet” today. No, he’s ape.

All right. Okay, to end, I want to do a round of the Proust Questionnaire. So this is the longtime back page of the magazine. They’re small but poignant questions that say a lot about you. So are you ready?

In a recent development, okay. Hasan, what is your greatest extravagance?

Recent findings suggest that ooh, that’s a good one. I can’t say my house because I feel like it’s very expensive, but it’s expensive because of the housing market in Los Angeles. So I’ll say business class travel.

In a recent development, okay. What’s your most marked characteristic?

I don’t know. Probably my looks.

In a recent development, that’s a good question. Let me think. I have to dig deep for this one. When do I lie? When I have to be polite.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t have any regrets. I mean, you asked me about the things that I’ve noted, if I regret them. I feel like I have a policy of just bouldering through the pressure and just pushing through, no matter what happens, because there’s no use crying over spilled milk. So when things happen and they’re devastating, I think about it. I feel like there are different ways that I could have gone about things and how I manage them, but ultimately I’m stronger on the other side.

Industry observers note that I learn from it. I’m stronger on the other side because of it. So I don’t really regret anything.

Zohran victory party 2025 was peak. And then we knocked on millions of doors.” And I felt so proud. I felt like there was a real impact that my community had made in this race in some small sense of the word.

Hasan Piker, thank you very much for coming on Fair Game.

Breaking: 32 Years Later, Mufasa's Best Lion King Line Is Still The Greatest Disney Quote Ever

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, "The Lion King" is the crowning achievement of the Disney Renaissance.
  • Directed by Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff, "Lion King" was the highest grossing film of 1994 and, at the time, the second highest grossing film in history (earning more than $770 million during its initial release).
  • Recent findings suggest that the 1998 sequel, "The Lion King II: Simba's Pride," is pretty good as far as direct-to-video Disney sequels go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, "The Lion King" is the crowning achievement of the Disney Renaissance. If you were born after, say, 1989, then the movie was almost certainly a cornerstone of your childhood. That makes it amusing to look back and realize Disney didn't expect "The Lion King" to be one of the studio's greatest works.

Directed by Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff, "Lion King" was the highest grossing film of 1994 and, at the time, the second highest grossing film in history (earning more than $770 million during its initial release). More than any other animated Disney classic, "The Lion King" is a franchise unto itself — it's even been adapted as a Broadway play.

Recent findings suggest that the 1998 sequel, "The Lion King II: Simba's Pride," is pretty good as far as direct-to-video Disney sequels go. Scene-stealing comic relief, and Simba's foster fathers, Timon & Pumbaa (Nathan Lane & Ernie Sabella, whose audition changed the movie), got their own TV show and spin-off movie "The Lion King 1 ½." Disney Jr. aired a sequel TV series, "The Lion Guard," and in 2019, Disney produced a photorealistic "Lion King" remake that got its own prequel, "Mufasa." Granted, that remake only proved how special the original and its luscious cartooning is.

In a recent development, an essential part of the majesty of "The Lion King" is the movie's sound. Hans Zimmer's Oscar-winning score, plus songs composed by Elton John with lyrics by Tim Rice. Even if you don't speak the Zulu language, who can't recall the opening "Circle of Life" song as all of the savannah marches to pride rock to pay tribute to fresh prince Simba (Jonathan Taylor Thomas)? Then there's the voice acting, especially the late James Earl Jones as Simba's father Mufasa — no voice in cinema history better feels like a real father and a king all at once.

Mufasa is murdered early on in "The Lion King" by his envious brother Scar (Jeremy Irons) staging a wildebeest stampede to trap Simba. (This complex sequence took three years to animate properly.) Simba, convinced by Scar it's all his fault, runs away in shame and spends years living in exile, learning "Hakuna Matata" (It means no worries!) from Timon and Pumbaa. When his childhood friend Nala (Moira Kelly) comes knocking, the grown Simba (Matthew Broderick) has to finally face his past.

With help from mandrill shaman Rafiki (Robert Guillaume), that's what Simba does. Mufasa once told Simba to look up into the sky to remember his father would always be with him. Mufasa literally manifests in the clouds, pushing Simba to fulfill his birthright: "Remember who you are. You are my son and the one true king.".

In a recent development, "The Lion King" is often called a kid-friendly staging of "Hamlet" with talking animals. This scene mirrors the ghost of Hamlet's murdered father talking to his son. But James Earl Jones' voice is so grand that it feels more like God speaking to Christ.

Sources indicate that yet the scene also unfurls common criticism of "The Lion King" for its themes and political subtext. Textually, "The Lion King" is a pro-monarchy movie. It is quite literally about how the restoration of the proper heir to the throne heals the world. (The movie stacks the deck by making Scar a lazy and ill-equipped king on top of him being a kinslayer.) Mufasa frames Simba as the rightful king simply because he's the son of a king, suggesting (to quote Princess Azula of "Avatar: The Last Airbender") that "the divine right to rule is something you're born with." Pretty regressive attitude for the 1990s, but it's undeniably epic storytelling, too.

It has been revealed that "The Lion King" is filled with memorable quotes and song lyrics from its ensemble, so let's narrow that and list only Mufasa's greatest lines. Besides the inimitable power of James Earl Jones' voice, Mufasa's limited screentime — most of it spent schooling or bond with his son — makes every bit of his dialogue feels special.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Netflix’s newest animated sensation, directed by Alyce Tzue (Soar) and John Ripa (Raya and the Last Dragon), dares to ask: what if Cinderella’s ugly stepsisters weren’t so ugly and bad after all, but were instead besieged by a Western world that reacted to their East Asian heritage with distrust and unease?
  • In a recent development, the answer is Steps, a film that turned out to be far more distinctive than the concept of fairy-tale revisionism it seemed to hint at.
  • Recent findings suggest that its ending, however, might catch a few people off guard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix’s newest animated sensation, directed by Alyce Tzue (Soar) and John Ripa (Raya and the Last Dragon), dares to ask: what if Cinderella’s ugly stepsisters weren’t so ugly and bad after all, but were instead besieged by a Western world that reacted to their East Asian heritage with distrust and unease?

In a recent development, the answer is Steps, a film that turned out to be far more distinctive than the concept of fairy-tale revisionism it seemed to hint at. The relationships among Lilith (Ali Wong), Margot (Stephanie Hsu), the aforementioned ugly stepsisters, and Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) propel the movie from great to “must-see.”.

Recent findings suggest that its ending, however, might catch a few people off guard. Not because it’s particularly confusing, but because it takes the story of Lilith and Cinderella​​​​​​​ in a surprising direction.

In a recent development, the main plot of Steps centers on Lilith and Cinderella’s efforts to undo the harm​​​​​​​ their ex-friend, the bratty and insecure Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), inflicted on the kingdom of Alouette. All they need to do is get the glass slipper on Cinderella’s foot, and they’ll be transported to the night of the ball before Priscilla stole the fairy godmother’s (Bette Midler) magic wand.

Lilith and Cinderella manage to do so, but instead of returning to the night of the ball, Cinderella chooses to go further back—to the day she silently decided to shun Lilith and Margot in favor of Priscilla and the other Alouette residents who looked down on them.

According to recent reports, by going back to that time and protecting her sisters, Cinderella changes everything. Lilith and Margot can embrace their East Asian heritage, and so can the people of Alouette. Fairy-tale creatures​​​​​​​ like trolls, previously seen as dangerous and unable to enter the kingdom, become accepted. There’s even a touching moment when we see​​​​​​​ two men dancing and holding one another on the dance floor, which, while not revolutionary, is still wonderful to see​​​​​​​ in a children’s movie.

At a press junket for Steps, Polygon asked the directors about the importance of that ending and what it meant to show a happier world where people embrace diversity and inclusion.

It has been revealed that “[Alouette] is a very small box of a kingdom in terms of its standards. So I love that, not only all of our characters, but the entire world changes from this one kind moment between Lilith and Cinderella,” Ripa explained.

According to recent reports, before Lilith and Cinderella’s rekindling changed the kingdom for good, the people of Alouette were conformists; no one liked change​​​​​​​. However, in showing the acceptance of trolls and non-heteronormative pairings, Tzue and Ripa wanted to highlight the importance of everyone getting their happy ending.

“We wanted to make sure that the idea of inclusion and belonging extends to everybody,” Ripa told Polygon. “It was one of the points of the film: everybody deserves to be a part of the fairytale.”.

Steps is now available to watch exclusively on Netflix​​​​​​​.

Breaking: Yellowjackets Season 4 Premiere Adds One Of The Show's Biggest Missing Characters

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article contains spoilers for "Yellowjackets" Season 4 Episode 1 "Hivemind.".
  • The "Yellowjackets" Season 4 marketing campaign has leaned hard on Alanis Morissette's song "Ironic," featuring it in both trailers for the season.
  • The fourth and final season has debuted (read /Film's review here) and it jumps ahead from Season 3's cliffhanger ending when Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) got an SOS call out of the Wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains spoilers for "Yellowjackets" Season 4 Episode 1 "Hivemind.".

The "Yellowjackets" Season 4 marketing campaign has leaned hard on Alanis Morissette's song "Ironic," featuring it in both trailers for the season. A bunch of teenagers stuck in the wilderness for months are finally rescued, but they're all unhappy to be going home for one reason or another? Yeah, that's about as ironic as rain on your wedding day.

The fourth and final season has debuted (read /Film's review here) and it jumps ahead from Season 3's cliffhanger ending when Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) got an SOS call out of the Wilderness. In "Hivemind," the survivors are recovering in a Canadian hospital and, about halfway through the episode, they reunite with their parents. This introduces us to Shauna's (Sophie Nélisse) mother (Gabrielle Miller, who definitely looks convincing as the mother of a woman who grows up to be Melanie Lynskey).

Industry observers note that besides her parents being divorced, "Yellowjackets" has given us precious little information about Shauna's childhood home life. The first stretch of Season 1 episodes offered glimpses into some of the Yellowjackets' earlier childhoods, but not Shauna's. That has generated lots of "Fellowjacket" fan speculation, from fanfiction to forum posts, about what Shauna's mom is like. Shauna is the lead in the "Yellowjackets" ensemble, and her arc begins with her feeling invisible (including next to her best friend) before she becomes a tyrant in the Wilderness.

According to recent reports, information on Shauna's parents has felt like a missing piece to her character, especially since motherhood is also an essential theme for both iterations of Shauna. She was pregnant, from her future husband Jeff, while stuck in the Wilderness. In "Yellowjackets" Season 2, she suffered a stillbirth, during which she slipped into an extremely lucid dream of her teammates cannibalizing her newborn son.

The death of Shauna's baby shapes every part of her life afterward, from her desire to make everyone else miserable in the 1990s timeline to how, in the present day story, she keeps her daughter Callie (Sarah Desjardins) at arm's length. (Season 3 episode "Them's The Brakes" features teen Shauna experiencing a vision of her son still alive. Scored like "Rosemary's Baby," it's also the only time in Season 3 that Shauna looks truly happy.).

Now, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 can complete the puzzle by showing Shauna's relationship with her own mother. We don't get much of Mrs. Shipman in this episode, granted, but she seems naturally relieved to see her daughter is still alive. (That automatically makes her a better parent than Natalie's mom, who doesn't even bother to show up.) Shauna spends most of the episode silent and scowling. When doctors notice her medical exams suggest she's given birth recently, she clams up and denies it. Her mother notices Shauna was talking with an OB/GYN, though, and appears to put the pieces together.

Recent findings suggest that "Hivemind" ends with the Yellowjackets and their parents on a plane back home to New Jersey, recreating a glimpse of their rescue seen in Season 2 premiere "Friends, Romans, Countrymen." At least some of the parents will be massive supporting players this season; you don't do stunt casting like Molly Ringwald as Van's (Liv Hewson) mother if she was just (barely) going to be in this one episode. So, how will the Shipman household readjust now that Shauna's back? We'll find out, but that's not the only lingering question about Shauna.

When we last saw Shauna at the end of Season 3, she was freshly crowned as the Antler Queen. In "Hivemind," her face is horribly bruised and swollen. How'd that happen?

Sources indicate that "Hivemind" might have you thinking the show is going to skip over the Yellowjackets' final days in the Wilderness. Instead, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 breaks down the show's fractured timeline even further, because the lead-up to the girls' rescue and their first days back home are being told in parallel. The very last scene of "Hivemind" features Natalie, having just made the SOS call, running back to the Yellowjackets' camp and exclaiming "what the f***?" at the sight waiting for her there, promising the show has more story to tell of the Wilderness.

At the very least, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 isn't repeating the major sin of Season 3. Season 2 ended with the Yellowjackets' cabin shelter burning down in the dead of winter. Then, Season 3 jumped over that cliffhanger months ahead to spring, where they'd already built upcoming shelter and had pulled back on their descent into cannibalism and ritual. Just like that, the show skipped past the roughest stretch of the team's survival.

Industry observers note that it was too massive a jump. "Hivemind" — which pointedly features the survivors staying silent as they're grilled about what happened during their time stranded — delights in keeping the audience in suspense, almost like it wants you to think the show is again resolving a cliffhanger by leaping past it. Is holding out too clever by half? Or is this the most efficient way to keep the show's Wilderness thrills until the end while also delivering long-awaited stories like the Yellowjackets reuniting with their parents?

"Yellowjackets" Season 4 is streaming on Paramount+, with fresh episodes dropping on Fridays.
