💡 Key Takeaways
  • Julio is a Senior Author for Collider.
  • Industry observers note that the best news for fans of spy thrillers this week isn't what you'd expect.
  • Gone are the golden years of cable TV, when viewers could expect their favorite shows to return year after year without fail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Julio is a Senior Author for Collider. He studied History and International Relations at university, but found his calling in cultural journalism. When he isn't writing, Julio also teaches English at a nearby school. He has lived in São Paulo most of his life, where he covers CCXP and other major events. Having loved movies, music, and TV from an early age, he prides himself in knowing every minute detail about the things he loves. When he is older, he dreams of owning a movie theater in a small countryside town.

Industry observers note that the best news for fans of spy thrillers this week isn't what you'd expect. While everyone was celebrating a new James Bond, MI5 actually had the biggest shake-up as Apple TV announced the renewal of Slow Horses for Seasons 9 and 10. You read that right — Season 6 has barely wrapped up, and viewers can already look forward to four more seasons of Jackson Lamb's (Gary Oldman) trademark grumpiness. This comes as a great surprise, not just the number of seasons itself, but given the greater circumstances. Back in September, Apple had already renewed Slow Horses for Season 8, and now, less than two months later, has confirmed an incredible Season 10 update. It's a really unprecedented move for any streamer, so is there a catch — or are things just that good at Slough House?

Gone are the golden years of cable TV, when viewers could expect their favorite shows to return year after year without fail. Getting lost in series like Friends, Supernatural, and Grey's Anatomy was a pleasure, but, with the dawn of the streaming age, it became harder and harder to find such long-running shows — so much so that people usually point to these behemoths of old when looking for long-term commitment on TV, as those titles remain available on most streaming platforms.

According to recent reports, because of the usual budget constraints, long-term casting commitments, and ever-changing business models, scripted live-action shows rarely go beyond six or seven seasons on streaming, so Slow Horses earning this type of renewal is completely unprecedented in the current landscape. Its now-confirmed 10-season run makes it Apple TV's longest-running series — a title it previously shared with For All Mankind, which is slated to end with Season 6.

According to recent reports, there are a few reasons that have resulted in Slow Horses getting this kind of treatment. Each season has only six episodes, making it much quicker to produce, and every season finale delivers a preview for the next batch of episodes. Most notable, though, is how well it performs among audiences and critics. On Rotten Tomatoes, every season of Slow Horses has consistently performed above 95%, so, from a business perspective, what's not to love about it?

On its own, this unexpected renewal is bound to keep Slow Horses and Apple TV at the top of viewers' minds for a while, especially with a new season set to premiere next year. Its consistent release schedule is another reason this series has performed so well since the beginning. (Longer gaps between seasons are another streaming staple, unfortunately.) To keep the pace, a quick production is important, but what's really vital is the fact that there has always been source material available to adapt for each new season.

It has been revealed that slow Horses famously adapts Mick Herron's Slough House book series, which presently comprises nine entries. From the beginning, each season has adapted one book, with the exception being Season 6 — which adapted two novels, Joe Country and Slough House. Right now, the expectation is that Season 7 will adapt Bad Actors and Season 8 will adapt Clown Town, Herron's most recent novel published in 2025.

Now that Slow Horses has been renewed for more, though, Seasons 9 and 10 don't yet have a published Herron novel to adapt — at least for now. The expectation is that a tenth Slough House novel will be confirmed, although there has been no confirmation as of this writing. Herron has previously mentioned that he already knows "why, when, and where Jackson Lamb dies," so it stands to reason that the Apple TV series won't run forever, and its end may be steadily approaching.

Even if Herron's tenth novel takes longer to reach publication than anticipated, there are still five Slough House novellas for the show to draw from, all compiled in Watch the Quiet Snow. It's still way too early to know where Slow Horses is headed in Seasons 9 and 10, but it seems unlikely that Apple TV would take such a bold step in renewing it without a clear plan.

Sources indicate that curiously, the timing of this renewal news couldn't have been better. Mere days prior, Olivia Cooke, who plays Sidonie "Sid" Baker, said in an interview that Season 8 would be Slow Horses' last, even mentioning that the cast has been "all melancholy" while filming. Apple TV's renewal immediately refutes this, adding another two seasons to the previously declared seventh and eighth back in September. (Hopefully, Season 8 isn't Cooke's last season, though.).

Finally, there is the "James Bond" of it all. Jack Lowden, who plays down-on-his-luck protagonist River Cartwright, was among the top contenders for 007, but although fans rooted for him until the very end, the role ultimately went to Robert Pattinson. Ironically, hoping to get out of Slough House for a better position in a government agency only to ultimately get shot down is such a Cartwright thing that we can almost hear Lamb laughing in the background. So far, only Oldman's return has been confirmed, but it's hard to imagine Slow Horses without the rest of Lamb's joes, no matter how many seasons the show ultimately runs for.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" adapts the story that fans have been waiting for since 2008, revealing how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor of Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), became the victor of the 50th Hunger Games. Haymitch's games were even more brutal than usual: as a special "quarter quell" game, each of the twelve districts had to offer up four children, not two. (Haymitch ends up in the games after one of the two District 12 boys originally chosen tries to flee and then is shot.).

One of the District 12 kids "reaped" alongside Haymitch is Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), the daughter of a candy shop owning family. A jewelry collector, Maysilee is the original owner of the Mockingjay pin that Katniss eventually comes to wear during the "Hunger Games" trilogy.

It has been revealed that now, this being a prequel where Haymitch's victory (as pyrrhic as it is) is assured, you should go into "Sunrise on the Reaping" knowing Maysilee doesn't walk out of that arena. Grace actually plays two roles in the film, the other being Maysilee's twin sister, Merrilee. Once Haymitch returns, during Maysilee's funeral, he has to see the very same face of the girl he failed.

In a recent development, viewers, too, might recognize Maysilee and Merrilee's shared face. Mckenna Grace is a prolific young actress with many film and TV (including voiceover) roles to her name. In just the past few years, she appeared in "Five Nights at Freddy's 2" as paranormal activity hunter Lisa, Clara in the Colleen Hoover adaptation "Regretting You," and Hannah Thurman in "Scream 7." Those recent roles only scratch the surface of her acting resume.

Born in 2006, Mckenna Grace is a recently graduated child actress; her first acting role was on the 2012 Disney XD series "Crash and Bernstein." Soon after she had a part on soap opera "The Young and the Restless" from 2013 to 2015 as Faith Newman. Her breakout film role was in 2017 Chris Evans vehicle "Gifted," where she played young math prodigy Mary Adler.

In a recent development, in the late 2010s, Grace found a niche playing child versions of main characters. She played young Tonya Harding in "I, Tonya," young Carol Danvers in "Captain Marvel," a young Sabrina Spellman in one episode of "The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina," and starred in Mike Flanagan's miniseries "The Haunting of Hill House" as a young version of Kate Siegel's character Theo Crain. This means she's played young versions of Margot Robbie, Brie Larson, and Kiernan Shipka. (Grace, who played Paige Swanson on sitcom "Young Sheldon," has mentioned she envisions Reese Witherspoon as the adult version of that character.).

From 2021 to 2022, during Seasons 4 and 5 of "The Handmaid's Tale," Grace played Esther Keyes, the abused teenage wife of a much older man. This role earned her an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Drama Series. 2021 was also the year that Grace starred in "Ghostbusters: Afterlife" as Phoebe Spangler, later reprising the role in 2024's "Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire.".

One of Grace's voiceover roles was playing a young version of Daphne Blake in the 2020 animated "Scooby Doo!" film "Scoob!" Fresh off of "Sunrise on the Reaping," she's going to play Daphne again, this time in live-action, in the upcoming TV series "Scooby Doo: Origins" due out in 2027.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is playing in theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pokémon Go is having a Pawniard Community Day event on Saturday, Nov. 21 from 2-5 p.m. in your local time. This event is indeed running alongside the "Dynamax Trails" event, and it begins right when Eternatus' stint in the morning ends.

It has been revealed that as expected with a Community Day event, Pawniward will spawn in huge numbers with a high chance for it to appear shiny. There are also several other bonuses and perks, which we've listed out below.

As per old research by the now-defunct website The Silph Road (via Wayback Machine), shiny rates on Community Days are about 1 in 24, which means that if you keep playing throughout the three-hour window, you should find quite a few shiny Pokémon.

If you’re short on time or Poké Balls, you can pop an Incense, then swiftly tap each Pawniard to check for shiny ones, running from any that aren’t shiny. Notably, any Pawniard you’ve already tapped will face where your player is standing, so that should help identify which ones you may have already checked.

It has been revealed that if you evolve Bisharp into Kingambit from 2-9 p.m. in your local time, it will learn the charged move Kowtow Cleave.

If you miss out on evolving it during this period, you will likely be able to evolve it during a Community Day weekend event in December to get Kowtow Cleave. If you don’t want to wait, you can use an Elite TM to get the move.

Usually, to evolve Bisharp into Kingambit, you'd need to set Bisharp as your buddy and beat 15 dark- or steel-type Pokémon in raids. However, for this Community Day, this requirement has been reduced heavily.

In a recent development, on Saturday, Nov. 21 from 2-9 p.m., you will only need to defeat 1 dark- or steel-type Pokémon in a raid with Bisharp as your buddy to evolve it into Kingambit. The evolution will still cost 100 Pawniard Candy, though. The Bisharp you are trying to evolve won't need to be used in the raid, it just needs to be set as your buddy Pokémon.

According to recent reports, with its Community Day move, Kingambit is actually a very strong dark-type attacker, only falling to Mega and shadow Pokémon. Definitely power one up and give it Snarl and Kowtow Cleave for success.

Its Community Day move also makes it a strong pick in PvP, specifically in the Great League. Run it with Low Kick, Iron Head, and Kowtow Cleave to make the most of it.

The following bonuses will be active during Pawniard Community Day:.

That said, you should definitely put your eggs in Incubators and pop an Incense and try to nab some powerful Pawniard.

If you can Mega Evolve Gyarados, Steelix, Scizor, Skarmory, Houndoom, Tyranitar, Sableye, Mawile, Aggron, Sharpedo, Absol, Metagross, Lucario, Greninja, or Malamar, you’ll score additional Pawniard Candy per catch.

Sources indicate that just the same as previous Community Days this year, the Lure Module bonus will be active for this event, too. Pawniard will continue to spawn from Lure Modules placed until 9 p.m., retaining their Community Day shiny rate and their chance to spawn with a Special Background.

This article contains spoilers for "MobLand" Season 2, Episode 10, "The Queen is Dead.".

Recent findings suggest that just when you think the Harrigans might catch a break, things blow up in their face. This time, a car literally blew up in the face of Tom Hardy's Harry Da Souza and his daughter, Gina Da Souza (Teddie Allen), during a frenetic "MobLand" Season 2 finale which almost ended without anyone kicking the bucket. In the episode's final moments, however, we witness what is surely the most shocking death in the entire series, when Joanne Froggatt's Jan Da Souza gets blown sky high thanks to Anson Boon's Eddie Harrigan.

It has been revealed that "Mobland" started life as a "Ray Donovan" spin-off, with Hardy set to play the English equivalent of Liev Schreiber's fixer — which he still sort of does. But his Harry is much darker, colder, and quietly ruthless. Alan Ritchson once compared playing Jack Reacher to playing an alligator waiting to strike. If that's true, then Hardy's Da Souza is a human nuclear warhead, sitting at the head of a ballistic missile and waiting to reduce the world to ashes. Thus far, despite the many challenges endured by the Harrigans in "MobLand" Season 2, he's managed to maintain his icy exterior. Now that his wife has gone up in flames, however, I get the feeling that reservoir of repressed rage is going to come flooding out in Season 3.

Industry observers note that season 2, Episode 10 has a deceptive title. When I first saw "The Queen is Dead" on the Paramount+ interface, I thought Maeve Harrigan's (Helen Mirren) days were numbered. But it turns out Jan was the one to pay the piper, and if anyone was going to go down in the season finale, she was surely the least deserving.

Industry observers note that early on, "Mobland" Season 2 proved that it hadn't lost a step in comparison to the first run of episodes. It might even have outdone Season 1, thanks in large part to Johnny Flynn as villain Frankie Cooper, who has been a non-stop delight to watch as the flamboyant, psychopathic London gangster. But the show's been firing on all cylinders from the very first episode of Season 2, in which Pierce Brosnan's Conrad Harrigan dual-wielded his way through an entire gang at a race track.

Industry observers note that since then, we've seen the Harrigan crime family come close to collapse. A campaign of violence waged by Frankie at the behest of corrupt U.S. Ambassador Katherine "Kat" McAllister (Janet McTeer) almost wiped out the Harrigans for good. In the season finale, however, Harry Da Souza pulls off an impossibly brilliant plan to finally oust Kat and capture Frankie, all while restoring his criminal employers to their former glory. But there's an unsettling aspect to the whole thing. By the end of the episode, nobody has died, leaving you with a sense that something truly terrible is about to happen.

The final scene sees Harry pull up to Conrad's home in the Cotswolds, leaving Jan and Gina Da Souza in the car. While Harry's inside, Gina and Jan leave the car for a chat. Meanwhile, Eddie Harrigan plants Semtex under the passenger seat and is just about to hit the detonate button when he receives a call from Colin Morgan's Kelly "Mad Dog" O'Connor. Startled, he drops the detonator just as poor old Jan gets back in the car. Boom. Harry and Gina watch the brutal scene unfold before their eyes. Eddie is surely a dead man.

Jan Da Souza's only real crime (apart from shooting Alex Fine's Donnie) has been sticking around while Harry Da Souza and his criminal cohorts engage in ever more dangerous conduct. Otherwise, she's about as innocent as a "MobLand" character can be.

Now, with "MobLand" Season 3 already in production, the question becomes, what sort of fallout will we see from this shocking turn of events? Surely, Eddie isn't making it out alive. The walls are already closing in on the Harrigan scion, and this cockup seals the deal.

Episode 5 of "MobLand" Season 2 showcased the dark side of a "Star Trek" legend when Colm Meaney portrayed an Irish gangster by the name of Medusa. Eddie was sent to kill Medusa but ultimately failed to carry out the hit, forcing Harry to finish the job. Now, Medusa's son, Mad Dog, is out for revenge. But with Eddie now having killed Jan, he'll surely face Harry's wrath, too. Can he really survive the vengeful rage of both Harry and Mad Dog?

In a recent development, meanwhile, there's Gina Da Souza, who has been teetering on the verge of embracing her father's criminal life all season. Jan's death will either push her away for good or prove to be her villain origin story. It might make for a decent storyline if Harry follows through on his promise to mentor Gina and turn her into a criminal force to be reckoned with. For now, we'll have to wait to see how things play out, but it's truly exciting to see "MobLand" continuing to be the best show it can be.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that it's rare for a franchise to get better after 4 or 5 movies, especially when they are prequels that explore questions no one needed answered.
  • In a recent development, and yet, when it comes to "Hunger Games," not only has the franchise improved with time, but the two spin-off prequels are arguably better than even the original series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The following post contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

It has been revealed that it's rare for a franchise to get better after 4 or 5 movies, especially when they are prequels that explore questions no one needed answered. It didn't work for "Star Wars," it didn't work for "Harry Potter," and it shouldn't work for "Hunger Games." At best, these prequels just introduced characters that don't matter in the large scheme of things because everything they do or accomplish gets erased in the original story, at worst they try so hard to answer questions no one cares about that it ends up tarnishing the original work.

In a recent development, and yet, when it comes to "Hunger Games," not only has the franchise improved with time, but the two spin-off prequels are arguably better than even the original series. The latest film, "Sunrise on the Reaping" deepens what came before, while introducing new characters that are as engaging as those we know and add to the larger worldbuilding of Panem. Or, as /Film's review puts it, "Beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end.".

Even if this movie doesn't have the compelling romance that was central to "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," it delivers a harrowing tale of rebellion. What's more, this is somehow the darkest movie in the "Hunger Games" series, and it's not even close. Not just in terms of deaths — though there are some truly brutal deaths in the movie (which are somehow tamer than the book!) — but also in the overall tone the movie explores. This is the "Hunger Games" equivalent of "Andor" or "Rogue One," a bleak tragedy about one man who dared stand up against a tyrannical government and paid for it with everything he had.

Industry observers note that the "Hunger Games" movies are full of death and suffering; it's part of the game. But "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes it to another level. Though it takes a long while before the nearly 3-hour runtime gets to the actual games, there's a feeling of hopelessness from the first moment. Early on, a kid gets shot for trying to escape the Reaping. Later, on the day of the opening ceremony, the youngest tribute from District 12, Loella, gets brutally killed in a chariot accident.

But it's not just the fact that there are plenty of deaths, or that they're horrible to watch. Sure, seeing poor Ampert get completely mauled by a swarm of cute forest animals and Maysilee Donner getting gored to death by birds is harrowing. The Capitol doesn't just kill children; it tortures them and pulls them apart and makes their parents watch.

Indeed, more than the deaths themselves, it's the meanness around them that makes this movie stand out. When Loella dies, it isn't a murder done by another tribute trying to get an advantage. Instead, it's an accident caused by Capitol audiences throwing flares at the parade circuit knowing full well it will cause the chariot horses to go berserk, because they want to see the tributes suffer. Compared to every other "Hunger Games" movie, the tributes are not only livestock sent to slaughter, or pawns in a political game. Here, they are subjects of absolute torture, playthings to be slowly toyed with and brutalized before getting discarded for the pleasure of others.

In a recent development, we especially see this in the presence of Ampert, whom we learn is only in the games as a punishment for his father Beetee's rebellious activities. Beetee is forced to mentor his own son and then watch him die.

Throughout "Sunrise on the Reaping," there is a sense of hopelessness and inevitability. We know that, eventually, the Hunger Games end and the Capitol falls — but the characters in the movie don't know that. At every turn, Haymitch and his allies see their every effort get squashed and mocked. Their attempts at leveling the playfield just a little bit are met with overwhelming force. Even before the games begin, Haymitch knows he'll never get to go back home because President Snow has personally seen to it that Haymitch dies for his insubordination during the opening ceremony.

Sources indicate that then we get to the third act, where the movie just becomes a cruel feel-bad experience, as Plutarch Heavensbee convinces Snow to let Haymitch survive to prolong his suffering. Haymitch is forced to watch Maysilee die brutally at the hands of waterbird mutts while he is virtually unscathed. Then, even after he wins the games, Haymitch discovers that the televised games were heavily edited to make him look selfish and cowardly, a traitor to every one of his allies, who won only because he was lucky. As if that wasn't enough, Haymitch has to see his family and his girlfriend die horrible deaths after he goes back home from the death games, in what's without a doubt the most nihilistic ending in the franchise.

In a recent development, it makes sense, however. "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place at a pivotal moment in the "Hunger Games" timeline, at the height of President Snow's power. We are far removed from the games being almost canceled due to lack of interest like in the previous movie, but also far removed from the simmering rebellion of the original movies. Here, Snow gets away with everything, and he relishes in the cruelty of his games.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Memory Ngulube joined Screen Rant in April 2024 as part of the Movies and TV team.
  • The science fiction genre has always prided itself on bringing stories that seem impossible to adapt to life.
  • According to recent reports, prime Video could soon have another ambitious space opera on its hands that has the potential to surpass the likes of sci-fi giants like The Expanse and Battlestar Galactica.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Memory Ngulube joined Screen Rant in April 2024 as part of the Movies and TV team. Since then, she has written for the Perennials and Streaming team, covering a wide range of topics from fresh releases to old movies and TV indicates. Memory is presently a Classic TV writer. Before joining Screen Rant, Memory was a freelance copywriter who specialized in email marketing and social media management. While she enjoyed her job, her true passion was always movies and TV. When she isn’t writing for Screen Rant, Memory can be found reading, baking (which is one of her passions), or watching her favorite K-drama.

The science fiction genre has always prided itself on bringing stories that seem impossible to adapt to life. Although the genre has thrived for myriad reasons, one of the most important aspects is how wellsci-fi highlights build their worlds. Several series have made this seem easy, when it is anything but. The Expanse, Battlestar Galactica, Foundation, and other sci-fi franchises have remained so influential in the space because they understand that a series with a world that doesn’t work won't grip audiences for long.

According to recent reports, prime Video could soon have another ambitious space opera on its hands that has the potential to surpass the likes of sci-fi giants like The Expanse and Battlestar Galactica. However, it has to get several elements of its source material right to achieve that admirable feat. In late 2024, Prime Video announced they would adapt James S.A. Corey’s expansive novel series, The Captive’s War, into a TV show.

Recent findings suggest that for fans of The Expanse, this news was welcome, but it also brought the genre-typical fear that the source material would be poorly adapted. However, The Captive's War could be Prime Video’s next flagship sci-fi series because it could give the streaming platform a chance to explore a different side of the genre. The source material for The Captive’s War series indicates that it is simply not going to be another version of The Expanse, but a TV show with an entirely new universe.

Sources indicate that prime Video’s adaptation of The Captive’s War could completely change how sci-fi is brought to life on streaming platforms. Following humanity after the alien Carryx empire invades the planet Anjiin and abducts a group of humans, The Captive’s War presents a staggering world.

The first book in the series, The Mercy of Gods, is a slow burn and takes a while to get going, but once it does, the story takes on a life of its own. Corey’s novels feature a variety of alien planets, rich biology, and strange aliens, particularly the Carryx. The novels’ extensive world creates a strong foundation for worldbuilding because some of these aliens are so fascinating. The Carryx, in particular, represents an entire civilization, social structures, and history that make Corey’s story even more interesting.

With the amount of information in the source material, it's kind of difficult to imagine how it will all come together. Even The Captive's War ​​​​​​authors Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck have acknowledged that the books feature spectacular alien species and complicated internal character perspectives that will make the television adaptation challenging. However, there is some hope. Prime Video’s adaptation of The Captive’s War is stacked with an incredible creative team.

Naren Shankar, who served as showrunner on The Expanse, and director Breck Eisner, who also worked on the space opera, will helm the adaptation of The Captive’s War. Shankar is attached as writer and showrunner, Eisner as director, while Abraham and Franck are also involved in writing the adaptation. They've already proven their mettle with The Expanse, so this creative dream team should help to quell book fans' fears about the adaptation.

Sources indicate that given that The Captive’s War and The Expanse were written by the same author, comparisons between the novels are inevitable. Though both stories demonstrate a perfect understanding of science fiction worldbuilding, they approach the concept from very different perspectives. Corey's hard sci-fi novel focuses primarily on humanity's expansion across the solar system, whereas The Captive's War imagines an enormous galactic civilization.

Political worldbuilding is the main reason The Expanse became so compelling, particularly through its exploration of the competing interests of Earth, Mars, and the Belt. Arguably, The Captive's War’s political maneuvering is even more interesting, especially because the story explores an alien civilization built around conquest, domination, and the exploitation of other species.

Recent findings suggest that all in all, The Captive's War’s setting is much larger than The Expanse and has more diverse characters. Despite the contrasts between these two stories, it is easy to agree that the worldbuilding in both of Corey’s literary works is what sets them apart.

10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth.
  • The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.
  • Industry observers note that an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?).

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

Industry observers note that an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

In a recent development, if your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for upcoming planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

Sources indicate that if you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous newly introduced reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

Sources indicate that if you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it's almost Thanksgiving, and as you prepare to fly home (well, depending on if planes are allowed in the sky when you need to do that), you might be feeling a weird sense of dread about sleeping in your parent's house next to their dusty Peloton on your old Spider-Man sheets. Why not binge-watch some stuff to deal with those feelings?

I've got you covered. There's a handful of newly introduced releases coming to major streaming platforms this week, and honestly? This is a pretty good handful. While major titles like "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" captivate people who decide to head to a movie theater and hang out there for a few hours, maybe you're looking for a scenario where you don't have to wear real pants and can pause whatever you're watching whenever the fancy strikes you. From one of the biggest horror hits in recent memory to the final season of a mystery box series to an offbeat biopic helmed by a Canadian comedy favorite, here are five movies or indicates to stream on Netflix, Disney+, Paramount+, Peacock, or HBO Max over November 20-22, 2026.

Besides the creepypasta horror hit "Backrooms," "Obsession" is the other film credited with keeping the horror genre young and fresh in 2026 — and it's not just because Kane Parsons and Curry Barker, the respective directors of those films, were born in 2005 and 1999. (As someone born in 1990, I admittedly do think about that a lot.) "Obsession," which is now available to watch on Netflix, and was completely devised by Barker, tells the story of Baron "Bear" Bailey (Michael Johnston), a young man carrying a torch for his platonic friend Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette, who may just end up earning an Oscar nod in 2027). After using a weird artifact called the One Wish Willow that he finds at an oddities store trying to get Nikki a gift, Bear wishes that Nikki would love him more than anything in the world ... and boy, does he get his wish.

Not only does Nikki really love Bear after the One Wish Willow takes effect, she seems unable to leave his side or focus on anything else — as if she's under some sort of hypnotic spell. "Obsession" is a dark, unsettling, and tightly directed horror film that interrogates Nikki's agency, Bear's distinct role in his own downfall, and what happens when you want someone to love you without actually knowing how they feel in the first place. "Obsession" is innovative, compelling, and one of the most popular movies in recent memory — and now, it's on Netflix.

In a recent development, when we last saw the titular Yellowjackets — a teenage soccer team stranded in the Canadian wilderness after a plane crash nearly two years prior — during the Showtime series' penultimate season in 2025, the teenagers in that wilderness were on the precipice of being rescued in the late 1990s. Meanwhile, in the more modern timeline, their adult counterparts are still trying to cover up whatever happened out in those woods. Now, in the fourth and final season (which earned a solid review right here at /Film), there are three timelines: one where the teenagers finish out their time in the wilderness, one after they've been rescued and dropped back into their "normal" lives in New Jersey, and that adult one, where all hell threatens to break loose as Shauna Shipman (Melanie Lynskey) continues to break bad after absolutely losing her s**t in Season 3.

Jasmin Savoy Brown, Liv Hewson, Sophie Thatcher, Sammi Hanratty, Courtney Eaton, and Sophie Nélisse make up the core of the teenage cast, while in the adult one, the always wonderful Lynskey is joined by Tawny Cypress, Christina Ricci, and even Oscar winner Hilary Swank (after former adult actors Lauren Ambrose, Juliette Lewis, and Simone Kessell exited at various points, though it's easy to imagine that they could reappear in Season 4 flashbacks at some point). As someone who's been watching this puzzle box show since the very beginning, I'll admit I have substantive doubts about "Yellowjackets" landing the plane (and it's not like its track record with these things is pretty great, if you consider the pun), but I'll definitely be watching Season 4 following its premiere on Paramount+ with Showtime on November 20, with fresh episodes airing weekly.

To call "Tony" a biopic feels ... sort of misleading. Directed by Matt Johnson (who recently wowed comedy nerds, a term I use affectionately, with "Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie" and cut his teeth on another biopic of sorts, "Blackberry"), the film follows a young Anthony Bourdain, played by the wry, excellent Dominic Sessa, as he learns a thing or two about life and proper oyster-shucking technique during a fateful summer in Providence, Rhode Island. Alongside a chef who never gets a proper name (Antonio Banderas) and who owns a small seafood place called "The Flagship," the titular Tony, who keeps insisting he's not an aspiring culinary expert but a writer with a fellowship (not true), pursues the girl of his dreams — photographer Nancy (Emilia Jones) — and gets into trouble with his fellow chef Sal (Leo Woodall) as he tries to figure out who he is and what he wants out of this experience.

Recent findings suggest that I didn't love "Tony" as much as many of my peers (see: /Film's own Bill Bria's review of the movie), but if you mentally remove the Bourdain of it all from the film and enjoy it as a showcase for Sessa's talents and Johnson's comedic timing, you'll probably get way more mileage out of this fresh, generally fun film. "Tony" is on HBO Max now, which makes sense, as its studio, A24, tends to premiere its movies there when they come to streaming.

Author Rick Riordan co-created the Disney+ series "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" for Disney+ along with Jonathan E. Steinberg ("Jericho"), and whether you're a fan of Riordan's original books, enjoyed the short-lived "Percy Jackson" film franchise, or have been waiting for this show to return since Season 2 concluded back in January of 2026, you'll be happy to hear that Season 3 premiered on Disney+ on November 20. In the inaugural season released in late 2023, the action follows the plot of Riordan's novel "The Lightning Thief" and sees the titular Percy, played by Walker Scobell, discovering that not only are Greek gods real, he has magical powers and can learn how to wield them at a place called Camp Half-Blood. After using the Empire State Building to reach Olympus at the end of Season 1, Season 2 catches up with Percy during the events of Riordan's book "The Sea of Monsters," which brings a bunch of elements of "The Odyssey" into play.

So, what about Season 3? It's set to follow Riordan's third novel, "The Titan's Curse," where Percy has to face off against Kronos and his army to rescue the goddess Artemis (Dafne Keen) and his friend Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries). The first two episodes of Season 3 dropped on Disney+ on November 20, with two episodes debuting every Friday throughout its run.

"Alien: Romulus" came out in 2024, and now, it's available to stream on Peacock. Fede Álvarez's entry into the storied "Alien" franchise features tons of rising stars like Cailee Spaeny, David Jonsson (who's gearing up to play the son of the late "Black Panther" star Chadwick Boseman's T'Challa in the Marvel Cinematic Universe), Spike Fearn, and Isabela Merced, and as it unfolds, we see half a dozen young colonists trying to navigate the deep recesses of space and finding dangerous creatures inside of an old space station. As orphan Marie Raines "Rain" Carradine (Spaeny) gathers the crew, including her adopted android brother Andy (Jonsson), her ex-boyfriend Tyler (Archie Renaux), his pregnant sister Kay (Merced), their cousin Bjorn (Fearn), and his adoptive sister Navarro (Aileen Wu), they encounter enemies left and right, leaving them shaken and fighting for their lives as they try to reach safety.

According to recent reports, when it comes to "Alien" movies, mileage may vary, but "Romulus" is a legitimately great entry to the property. (Just look at that unbelievable cast!) It's also streaming on Peacock now, so the movie can creep you out from the comfort of your own home.

Disney has announced a major milestone coming next month in its plans to merge the Disney+ and Hulu apps, which will be “fully unified” into Disney+ soon.

Today Disney reported its quarterly earnings and gave an enhancement on plans to merge Disney+ and Hulu into one app.

According to recent reports, live TV and premium add-ons were the final Hulu features that hadn’t yet been imported to the Disney+ app. But by adding those capabilities into Disney+, the app unification will be “complete.”.

The branding is going to get messed up. People look at Disney+ and Hulu as two different unique things. If you make the name just Disney+ people will think what Hulu historically provided is gone.

I find the current integration of Disney+ and Hulu cumbersome. I always find myself going back to my Hulu app to watch content. This may end up being a terrible move for them.

The ultimate goal of unifying everything in Disney+, though, will be accomplished soon.

Also in the earnings report, Disney noted that creator content will start appearing in the Disney+ app in December. This is related to the company’s deal with TikTok that debuted after its previous OpenAI deal fell apart when Sora was killed off. The Disney+ app will also get “more vertical video, live sports, and podcasts” soon too, Disney said.

Industry observers note that what do you think of the plans for the Disney+ app? Let us know in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that calvin and Hobbes creator Bill Watterson is a genius.
  • While this selection only scratches the surface of what made Calvin and Hobbes such a brilliant creation, here are nine comic strips from the 1990s that illustrate Watterson’s incredible range as an artist.
  • According to recent reports, one of Watterson’s recurring themes in Calvin and Hobbes was his unabashed love and admiration for the natural world, a respect he channeled right into his two leading characters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that calvin and Hobbes creator Bill Watterson is a genius. Over the course of ten years spanning more than 3,000 comic strips, he developed two truly irresistible characters that are still beloved by millions. There was a lot behind the success of Calvin and Hobbes, but I think part of the reason why Watterson is still so widely respected is that he was an incredibly versatile artist who managed to do a lot of different things in an artform that can sometimes be limiting.

While this selection only scratches the surface of what made Calvin and Hobbes such a brilliant creation, here are nine comic strips from the 1990s that illustrate Watterson’s incredible range as an artist.

According to recent reports, one of Watterson’s recurring themes in Calvin and Hobbes was his unabashed love and admiration for the natural world, a respect he channeled right into his two leading characters. Watterson returned to this subject many times and the points he made were always thoughtful. This one, from April 1992, is especially touching, as Calvin laments that humans have lost their “awe of nature.”.

Sometimes, Watterson seemed to use Calvin and Hobbes as an outlet for whatever big, philosophical questions were on his mind at the time. In this comic strip, Calvin and Hobbes have an in-depth conversation​​​​​​​ on the nature of luck. The best part about it is that they have it in a little wagon, careening down a giant hill. Calvin lands in some pricker bushes, which he seems to think is pretty unlucky.

Industry observers note that calvin often spoke well above the intelligence of a 6-year-old, but these comics were balanced out by adventures where Calvin is just being an imaginative little kid, like in this Sunday strip from 1995 where Calvin imagines meeting an alien who camouflages himself as Calvin. The real Calvin then goes to school pretending to be the alien, which lands him in the principal’s office.

It has been revealed that in addition to mastering the joke-a-day format demanded of comic strips, sometimes Watterson would tell longer stories which spanned several days or even a couple of weeks. For example, when his arch-nemesis, Rosalyn the babysitter, came over, their encounters often became epic sagas full of twists and turns​​​​​​​, like the story from 1990 in which Calvin drove Rosalyn nuts​​​​​​​ pretending to be Stupendous Man.

Industry observers note that there were many Calvin and Hobbes strips which were incredibly heartfelt, like this tender comic from 1993 that merely reveals a day in the life of Calvin and Hobbes, with both longing to be reunited​​​​​​​. The best part about it is its complete lack of dialogue.

Sources indicate that while Watterson was capable of being thoughtful and heartfelt, some of his comic strips featured a surprisingly dark sense of humor. This side of him was best captured by the strips depicting Calvin’s snowman sculptures, which always showed snowmen going through horrific things.

Sources indicate that this strip, from Jan. 21, 1991, contains​​​​​​​ three snowman sculptures in one. The first shows a snowman being shot with a cannon, the second a snowman being buried alive, and the third a snowman being hanged by a noose.​​​​​​​ That last one is especially hard to picture alongside more child-friendly newspaper comics like Peanuts and The Family Circus.

Like most other comic strips, Calvin and Hobbes had a simple drawing style, but occasionally Watterson would find an excuse to do something in much more detail, like when Calvin would pretend he was a Tyrannosaurus rex, like he does in this Halloween-themed strip from 1993.

For the most part, Watterson worked within the traditional bounds of newspaper comic strips, but he never let those traditional rectangles hold him back from a really creative idea. His dinosaur comics were a great example of this, as he liked to make his dinosaurs as big as possible. Another example of Watterson breaking the traditional format is this August 1995 strip, in which Calvin had​​​​​​​ an extended internal monologue about his parents being aliens.

Of course, a collection of perfect Calvin and Hobbes comics from the 1990s would not be complete without Watterson’s final comic, which ran on Dec. 31, 1995. This open-ended sendoff was beautifully understated and deeply poignant. It could not have been better.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that that’s why I drove the Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design for the second time this year — just to convince myself that there are better 3-row midsize SUVs out there.
  • But after another week behind the wheel, I can tell you firsthand that judging the Ioniq 9 by its cover is a mistake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quite frankly, the Hyundai Ioniq 9 gets a bad rap for the way it looks. In fact, I noted in my 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 review that the design is an “odd mashup featuring a curvy front bumper with an even stranger-looking arched rear.” It’s one of the last SUVs I’d expect to win any beauty awards.

Sources indicate that that’s why I drove the Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design for the second time this year — just to convince myself that there are better 3-row midsize SUVs out there. I’ve spent more time testing 3-row SUVs than any other vehicle type this year, with models like the Kia Telluride, Volvo XC90, Volkswagen Atlas, and Lucid Gravity getting my seal of approval.

But after another week behind the wheel, I can tell you firsthand that judging the Ioniq 9 by its cover is a mistake. Here’s what I realized.

Best long distance driving efficiency.

Best short distance driving efficiency.

It has been revealed that as with most vehicles, fuel economy and efficiency tend to dwindle over time — which is why I’m shocked that the Ioniq 9 is an exception. I was already impressed by the 3 mi/kWh average I got when I drove it last year, yet my second run delivered even better results.

Industry observers note that across 130.5 miles of mixed driving, my second go-around with the Ioniq 9 yielded an impressive 3.3 mi/kWh. What surprised me even more was the substantial improvement in city driving, where I recorded a peak tally of 4.5 mi/kWh — up from my previous best of 3.8 mi/kWh.

Considering it’s marketed as a three-row family hauler, it’s remarkable that the Ioniq 9 can post numbers like this. That extra efficiency is critical, too: while this trim carries an EPA-estimated range of 311 miles, averaging 3.3 mi/kWh puts its real-world range closer to 363 miles.

I’ll admit I was harsh on the Hyundai Ioniq 9’s styling the first time around. While it certainly takes cues from the subcompact Hyundai Kona, I argued that it was an odd mashup that was confused about what aesthetic it was trying to go after.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

After spending another week with it, though, its unconventional look slowly grew on me — even if that appreciation is mostly isolated to the front of the EV. That’s due to Hyundai’s signature Parametric Pixel LED light bar, which stretches across the nose like something straight out of a sci-fi movie. Those individual blocks give it a retro look that becomes even more dazzling from dusk into the night. In a sea of generic crossovers, this one certainly commands road presence.

That remarked, I still haven’t come to terms with the back half of this electric SUV. That tapered, upright rear end remains the hardest pill to swallow, giving it the look of a boat tail. Despite this, I now appreciate that the shape is doing the heavy lifting to make it aerodynamic — and subsequently boosting its efficiency.

It has been revealed that whether I’m making a quick stop at the local grocery store or on my 30+ mile commute to work, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 doesn’t skimp on the comforts. Step inside, and it’s clear Hyundai prioritized first-class comfort for the people riding up front and in the middle.

For example, the plush H-Tex seats strike a great balance of softness and support — which, for the driver, includes extra pampering courtesy of Hyundai’s Ergo Motion seat. When activated, it slowly adjusts the firmness of the cushion, sort of like getting a mini massage while driving, all to deter fatigue on longer hauls.

Still, the real VIP treatment belongs to the second-row captain’s chairs. With both heating and ventilation, plus power-reclining backrests and extendable footrests, they turn the middle row into a rolling lounge. However, the third row leaves more to be desired. Although I still appreciate having the extra seating capacity in a pinch, the legroom back there is practically nonexistent for adults — so I’d much rather keep that rear bench folded flat to make way for more trunk space.

At nearly $80,000 as tested, the Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design comes loaded with just about every luxury and tech perk anyone could ask for — and rightfully so.

It has been revealed that ​I still absolutely love Hyundai's adaptive cruise control, which makes long drives bearable and includes a dedicated lane-centering button on the steering wheel that also happens to work on local roads. Adding to that is a crisp Head-Up Display that projects my speed and navigation right onto the windshield.

​Changing lanes is effortless thanks to the Blind-Spot View Monitor (which streams a live camera feed straight into the digital gauge cluster) and a digital rearview mirror that offers a wider field of view than a conventional glass mirror.

​Back-seat passengers get plenty of love, too, with built-in rear side-window sunshades, a massive panoramic sunroof, and dazzling customizable ambient lighting that sets an upscale mood after dark.

​There’s also practical utility in the form of a handy 120V outlet accessible right in the trunk, letting me power laptops, tailgating gear, or small appliances straight off the SUV’s battery.

At nearly $80,000 as tested, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design is easily one of the most expensive vehicles in Hyundai’s entire lineup — and that price tag has long made me a skeptic.

​Yet spending a second week behind the wheel proved that judging it at face value is a mistake. Between its even better real-world efficiency, spacious cabin suited for families, and a laundry list of thoughtful luxury features, the Ioniq 9 delivers where it counts most: a family hauler that's rich in utility and backed by an efficient drive.

In a recent development, it's officially the end of an era for Paramount+'s acclaimed psychological thriller as its fourth and final season premieres with a deadly latest chapter. As one of ScreenRant's top new shows to binge-watch on Paramount+ this weekend, this star-studded thriller has also been one of the platform's most celebrated shows of the 2020s, earning a 90% Rotten Tomatoes score and 10 Emmy nominations, including two Outstanding Drama Series nominations. That stated, the beginning of the end is already underway following its season premiere this Friday.

Yellowjackets season 4 just premiered this week on November 20, exclusively on Paramount+, marking the highly anticipated release of the confirmed final season of the acclaimed psychological thriller series. The final season of Yellowjackets ends an era that began in 2021 and may end up being the final installment of the entire thriller franchise, although the series' showrunners have both expressed interest in developing a potential spinoff series in the near future. If not, Yellowjackets fans will be left with its original 4-season, 39-episode run.

It has been revealed that yellowjackets season 4 returns with a changed format that is set to deliver a strong conclusion to the celebrated series. The previous three seasons followed the survivors of a plane crash over two separate timelines, but now will feature three different timelines in season 4, one set in the present day, and two set in the 1990s before a significant event. Without getting too deep into spoiler territory, Yellowjackets season 4 brings the crash survivors home to reunite with their families and return to civilization after 19 months in the wilderness. To discover who, exactly, returns home, you'll have to watch.

Sources indicate that this new timeline offers a fascinating new lens for many of the characters who return home after the wild events that occurred throughout the previous three seasons. The social order between the characters while stranded was completely flipped on its head from normal life, meaning that each of the returning survivors will have a massive adjustment and reintegration period while also processing traumatic incidents and even trying to conceal instances of misconduct.

Despite their best efforts, certain characters may have to come to terms with their past actions and face the consequences in one final reckoning, which is a driving force of the mystery and tension throughout season 4's fresh timeline. While the only objective was staying alive by any means necessary in the wilderness, the power dynamics are set to shift, creating an entirely new psychological dynamic.

With Yellowjackets season 4 already revealed as the final installment, the series is now tasked with providing satisfying conclusions across not two, but three, timelines, no longer being able to rely on season-ending cliffhangers to maintain suspense between seasons. This will be the biggest make-or-break test for the acclaimed Paramount+ series and will determine how the series truly stacks up when it's all stated and done. Plenty of celebrated series, including the thematically similar hit Lost, were unable to tie up all the loose ends before their finales, which is a legitimate risk for Yellowjackets heading into its farewell tour.

One of the biggest mysteries Yellowjackets season 4 has to answer is what happened just before the survivors were rescued and brought home. This aspect was never fully explained at the end of Yellowjackets season 3 and must be resolved in the remainder of the pre-rescue timeline. The series also has to link the latest post-rescue timeline to the present day, portraying how the teen characters came to be adults. It will also be interesting to discover what, if any, secrets from the wilderness make it out, and how all that drama will unfold. There are certainly high expectations for Yellowjackets season 4 to stick the landing as the series officially comes to an end on Paramount+.

How to hide the new macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (323 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override.
  • According to recent reports, if you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar.
  • I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

According to recent reports, if you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:.

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false.

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:.

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR.

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future patch.

Recent findings suggest that not a fan of this on macOS 27.3 beta 2. Terminal command + reboot removed.sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false pic.twitter.com/HVvWdInqPh.

#51400. Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’

Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived).
  • “The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts.
  • It has been revealed that “ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived). On Wednesday night, Hill spoke before a packed screening at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and looked back on the movie that jump-started not only his screenwriting endeavors, but a directing career that would ultimately include classics like “The Warriors,” “48hrs.,” and “Streets of Fire.” Related Stories Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here Is A24 Finally Massive Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

“The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts. “The Getaway” was, appropriately enough, selected by the writers branch, and screenwriter and Academy Governor Larry Karaszewski was on hand to introduce the movie and moderate the pre-screening discussion with Hill. Karaszewski, a longtime “Getaway” enthusiast who carried newspaper ads from the movie around in his wallet when he was 10 years old, pointed out that Hill changed the entire architecture of screenwriting when he burst onto the scene in the early 1970s.

It has been revealed that “ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski mentioned. “We have an award show here at the Oscars called the Sci-Tech Awards, where they give awards to things that silently change the industry and advance them into the future. I really feel that Walter Hill did that in screenwriting, but it wasn’t a technical advancement. It was a literary advancement. He changed what a page should look like as a screenplay and what it could feel like to read it.” Karaszewski went on to illustrate his point by projecting pages from Robert Bolt’s “Doctor Zhivago” screenplay and Walter Hill’s “Hard Times” side by side on the screen.

In a recent development, “You don’t even have to read [Bolt’s script], just look at it,” Karaszewski remarked, pointing out the dense blocks of words compared to Hill’s lean, spare page. “You’re looking at monoliths. It’s dense, and there are camera moves and references to things you would never see on screen. Walter Hill taught screenwriters that you can strip all that away. You can still direct on the page, but not by calling for specific camera movements — just by saying what you’re seeing. Walter’s scripts are made out of short sentences and white space. He looked at the placement of each line as part of the storytelling. He turned the carriage return into an art form.”.

As Karaszewski welcomed Hill to the stage, he pointed out that “The Getaway” — a smart, terse tale of a couple (Steve McQueen and Ali MacGraw) on the run after their involvement in a botched bank robbery — represented the emergence of Hill’s developing voice. “You’ll already see the beginnings of that remarkable style, the economy, the precision, the sense that every line is pushing you toward the next image.” Yet, as Hill revealed in his lively conversation with Karaszewski, the ruthless efficiency of the pacing and the concentrated emotional impact of “The Getaway” were not easily arrived at.

In a recent development, “I think it’s much harder to adapt than it is to write an original, which is the reverse of the normal theory,” Hill said. “With an original, it’s just you at your desk with the typewriter or pen. When you’re adapting, that almost always means that somebody else owns it, so you’re not simply writing based on your own opinions about what should be in and what should be out, but there’s the producer’s opinion, and the studio’s, and the actor’s. There were all these political currents that one had to navigate.”.

One such political current came from megastar McQueen, who didn’t interfere much with Hill’s writing but did have one caveat that amused the screenwriter. “He wanted to play a reasonably sympathetic outlaw,” Hill stated. “That was not in the Thompson sensibility. So we already had a disparity, but the producer wanted to keep Steve happy.”.

Sources indicate that “The Getaway” began as an assignment not for Peckinpah, but for Peter Bogdanovich, who was white-hot coming off of successes like “The Last Picture Show” and “What’s Up, Doc?” Bogdanovich didn’t last long, however, given his clashes with McQueen and McQueen’s power as the film‘s star. “I couldn’t imagine two more diverse sensibilities than Steve and Peter,” Hill stated, noting that he had his own disagreements with Bogdanovich over the movie’s tone but wasn’t in a position to argue. “You’ve got to remember, I was nobody. I had one screen credit. And these were substantial players.”.

In a recent development, the substantial players included not only Bogdanovich and McQueen, but MacGraw, hot off of the smash hit “Love Story.” MacGraw was pushed into the movie by her husband, Paramount studio chief Robert Evans, which Hill found amusing given the way everything played out. “I’m going to tread lightly here,” Hill stated of the behind-the-scenes melodrama involving MacGraw leaving Evans when she fell in love with McQueen. “When the material was optioned and I was hired, Bob saw the movie as a fabulous idea for Steve and Ali. It didn’t work out so well for him.”.

According to recent reports, after Bogdanovich and McQueen butted heads, Bogdanovich was let go and Peckinpah, who McQueen had enjoyed working with on “Junior Bonner,” came in to take his place. “We were very lucky to get such a talented guy, obviously,” Hill remarked. “I thought of him then and I think of him now as one of the great directors with a very unique sensibility. I was very privileged to work with him — which doesn’t mean he and I agreed about everything.”.

Recent findings suggest that hill’s biggest disagreement with Peckinpah had to do with a scene in which MacGraw’s character considered killing McQueen before turning the gun on his nemesis — and the man with whom MacGraw had gone to bed to secure McQueen’s early release from prison. This was a scene carried over from the book, which was darker and more paranoid than what made it to the screen given McQueen’s mandate that he be sympathetic. Hill felt that the moment no longer worked now that the relationship between McQueen and MacGraw was softer and more relatable in the novel.

“I thought that for the movie we were trying to make, you might forgive your wife for sleeping with a bad man to do a very good thing for you,” Hill mentioned. “That seemed to be to be conceivable. But if your wife fell into cahoots with the bad guy and actually was thinking about killing you and actually turned the gun on you before she decided to shoot the other guy…this did not track for me. But this is the screenwriter’s dilemma: you either talk the director into your point of view, or you make the change that he wants — or somebody else will. Those are your choices.”.

Hill lost the argument but liked the movie Peckinpah made in the end. “He staged it beautifully,” Hill stated. “He shot it beautifully. It’s got one of Steve’s best performances. And the movie turned out to be his greatest hit. He used to call me every once in a while after I became a director and say, ‘Write me another one.'” Ironically, it was the success of “The Getaway” that put Hill in a position where didn’t have to write for other directors anymore.

Recent findings suggest that “Larry Gordon had a producing deal to make low-budget movies at Columbia,” Hill said. “He would give young writers a chance to direct, because he said, ‘Even if they’re no good as directors, at least we’ll get a good script. Most of the directors I’m working with aren’t any good anyway.'” Gordon gave Hill the opportunity to direct “Hard Times,” and the rest was history. Aside from kicking off Hill’s directing career, the collaboration became the first of many between the two men. “He’s a wonderful guy and a wonderful producer.”.

In a recent development, now in his 80s, Hill continues to write and direct (his last film was the exquisite character-driven Western “Dead for a Dollar“), plying his trade in the world of graphic novels in between film projects. “I’ve had four of them published in France,” Hill said, joking that the only one published in America was “the least good of them,” but promising another one on the way. “You’ve got to keep your hand in somehow.”.

It has been revealed that for AI features that depend on server-based models, each device running iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, or macOS 27.3 will have limited daily access to advanced AI features. These include complex Siri AI requests, Image Playground, certain Photos app editing tools, and more.

The only iCloud+ tier that doesn’t include higher limits is the $0.99/month strategy.

Recent findings suggest that I did offer alternatives like backing to your Mac or external SSD, but to have a proper backup safety system you need 1-2 backups at home and one off site (ie. friends house, storage facility, etc.) and you would have to be consistent with your backups and drop offs. Most people don’t have the time so they do iCloud, same as I.

iCloud+ already provided far more than just increased cloud storage, but with iOS 27.3 it’s set to be an asset for AI power people too.

According to recent reports, the changing of the clocks has taken its toll on my sleep this Fall. After long evenings bathed in artificial light, I've been feeling more wired than tired at bedtime. But thanks to one surprising gadget, lately I've been more consistent with my bedtime – and that's a good thing as studies link sleep consistency with better life expectancy.

According to recent reports, now that I’m prioritising a consistent sleep routine, I’m also waking up less through the night. So what is this surprising gadget? A red light face mask. Were you expecting something different? Mask aside, red light is said to accentuate the production of sleep hormones.

However, sceptical that I’ve been lulling myself to sleep with nothing more than a placebo effect, I called on double-boarded sleep medicine specialist Dr. Chris Winter to ask whether the science around red lights sleep benefits checks out. Here's what he said...

Due to my job, I have a collection of gadgets to reach for when it comes to bedtime – the Ozlo Sleepbuds, Hatch Sleep Clock and the Oura Ring 5 included.

But one that's really surprised me lately is the Bob and Brad PhysioFace Light Therapy Mask, available for $169.99 (was $199.99) at Amazon.

I've been using the mask, chiefly marketed for skincare purposes, as part of my bedtime routine and it's helped me put down my phone and get to sleep on time.

It has been revealed that as much as I love my Hatch clock, I don't love that I have to use my phone to alter settings. That's the beauty of this red light mask – it’s independent from my phone (there's no app to download) with control buttons attached to the device itself.
