That means I am actually making my bedroom a phone-free space and instead focusing on winding down for a great night's sleep.

It's hard to quantify exactly how well the red light mask is improving my sleep quality. But one thing is for sure: by the time I remove the mask, I feel sleepy and it never takes me long to dose off into a deep sleep.

According to my Garmin sleep timeline, I've reached deep sleep within half hour of dropping off, and continue to cycle through healthy sleep stages.

But what does Dr. Winter think? "It’s possible that taking a quiet break for your skincare routine is helping you unwind, particularly if it replaces scrolling or other stimulating activities.

"But feeling that you’re sleeping better doesn’t tell us whether the benefit is coming from the light itself, the routine, or something else.

"I would view it as a potentially relaxing part of your routine — not a proven sleep treatment," the board-certified neurologist cautions.

Industry observers note that white and blue light from screens is bad news for sleep. But as the nights draw in, a lot of our evenings are powered by these types of light. This winter, I’ve been making a conscious effort to swap my overhead light for the sundown setting on my Hatch Sleep Clock. I've also been swapping doomscrolling with reading time while wearing my red light mask.

In a recent development, 20 minutes prior to bedtime – after writing my do-to list for the following day and shutting off my phone for the night – I pop the mask on in bed and start reading a book. The 10-minute timer on the mask ensures I read for at least 10 minutes before drifting off.

The mask has three light modes with different colored lights. I've been using the BOOST mode that combines red light and near-infrared light. As well as supposedly boosting skin health, red light is associated with relaxation and there is some science associating it with improved sleep quality.

Although evidence is limited, research by Chinese scientists published in the National Library of Medicine, suggests red light influences melatonin secretion, improving sleep initiation.

Dr. Winter also referred to a 2026 review of five randomized trials that found a modest improvement in self-reported sleep quality when red light was introduced. "But the authors emphasized that the evidence was limited and imprecise," he notes.

Additionally, red light face masks, like my Bob and Brad model, are built to increase collagen production. They do this by penetrating the skin with red light, which stimulates the cells responsible for collagen synthesis. Besides improving skin elasticity, collagen can also improve sleep. A 2024 study concluded that increasing collagen at bedtime reduces sleep fragmentation.

Placebo or not, the mask has helped me prioritise a consistent bedtime routine over the past two weeks, and sleep better than I was immediately after the clock change.

I’ve been writing about sleep for over two years, and one thing I’ve learnt is that your sleep routine must be personal. A gadget or habit that works for someone else may not work for you.

Industry observers note that if you’re struggling to sleep, you may need to try a few different methods or technologies before you hit on one that clicks. But one piece of advice sleep experts all agree on is that you need a relaxing prelude to sleep if you want to clock quality ZZZs.

It has been revealed that A nighttime routine involves practising the same sequence of activities in the run up to your bedtime, helping prepare both your brain and body for sleep. In time, and with consistency, your body clock will come to recognise this routine as a signal to sleep, helping you drift off easily.

It has been revealed that dr. Winter explains: "A bedtime routine creates a predictable opportunity to step away from work, screens and other stimulating activities, rather than expecting your brain to switch off the moment your head hits the pillow. Pairing that wind-down period with a consistent sleep schedule and lower lighting helps support your body’s sleep-wake rhythm.".

This routine should be "simple, enjoyable and easy to repeat" and can include activity you find relaxing, be that a dark shower, mediation, reading, stretching or simply listening to calm music.

"You don’t need an elaborate checklist or expensive equipment—the goal is to wind down, not give yourself another assignment," advises the host of the Sleep Unplugged podcast.

"Think of the routine as making room for sleep, not forcing it to happen.".

‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.
  • Recent findings suggest that at this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two.
  • More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.].

Recent findings suggest that at this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’ Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here.

According to recent reports, the word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

Industry observers note that in both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

For her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

According to recent reports, but when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

Recent findings suggest that when Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

In a recent development, even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

Recent findings suggest that she also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

It has been revealed that if these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

While HBO Max has a strong slate of latest reveals to watch this weekend, Sharp Objects is a guaranteed winner that is worth the investment, especially due to its complex and masterful character design.

It has been revealed that sharp Objects is based on the acclaimed 2006 debut novel by Gillian Flynn, best known for Gone Girl, and is considered a quintessential modern Southern Gothic psychological thriller. Amy Adams stars as Camille Parker, a nuanced and multifaceted protagonist who Adams brilliantly brings to life on screen. Camille is a troubled investigative journalist who returns to her hometown in rural Missouri to look into two cases involving young girls in the community. One was murdered, while another remains missing. Camille harbors a variety of self-destructive tendencies, including alcoholism and self-harm, and is also haunted by a mysterious childhood trauma.

Recent findings suggest that similar to Kate Winslet's Mare Sheehan in Mare of Easttown and Matthew McConaughey's Rust Cohle in season 1 of True Detective, Camille is an excellent investigator despite her personal issues, which stem from unresolved wounds. Camille reluctantly arrives in her hometown to report on the aforementioned crimes, but inadvertently confronts her past, which dives into a dysfunctional family system.

Adams was challenged with personifying Camille's elaborate inner life as described in Flynn's novel for the series, which she was able to accomplish with great emotional effect. Despite being the hero of the story, Camille behaves quite inwardly, contrasting the standard archetype of most crime thriller protagonists. She does this while hinting at a deeper narrative meaning for her character from start to finish, making her performance a true masterclass in both development and execution.

Camille's internal layers are best portrayed through her relationships with her family members, particularly her mother Adora, played by Patricia Clarkson, and her half-sister Amma, played by Eliza Scanlen​​​​​​. Adora is well known in Camille's hometown for her wealth and influence, which has enabled her to be a controlling force over Camille throughout her childhood. Adora is also quite duplicitous, switching between a pleasant public demeanor and a cold, manipulative private persona.

Even as an adult, Camille's self-destructive behaviors can all be traced back to this toxic dynamic with her mother, which provides additional tension throughout Sharp Objects that is even more compelling than the ongoing murder mystery. As for Amma, she is also stuck in Adora's web of manipulation, behaving innocently in her presence and rebelliously outside of her view. While Camille internalized much of her trauma, Amma externalizes it by acting out, often recklessly.

Also included in this dysfunctional family tree is Amma's father and Camille's stepfather, Alan, played by Henry Czerny, who adopts a mostly passive presence around Adora with the intention of avoiding conflict. This leaves Camille with little support within her family, as the other two people closest to Adora are all responding differently to her emotional cruelty as a means of protection and survival within the family system. From a psychological lens, Sharp Objects is expertly crafted and offers a wealth of character development on HBO Max.

Crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other reveals mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's tech giant town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the latest sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated proposal to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

In a recent development, tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates fresh maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Manufacturer all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other indicates on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

Industry observers note that the great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Sources indicate that adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a newly introduced adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

Latest Update: Steven Spielberg’s 13-Part Sci-Fi Series Is So Good, You’ll Finish It in One Weekend

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few things are as creepy as children in horror films and TV series.
  • According to recent reports, the Whispers opens with a playful scene, as children in a yard run through sprinklers, blow bubbles, and do what kids do.
  • What the game is, no one knows, but it involves Harper collecting tools and going up into the treehouse, where she's not supposed to be alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few things are as creepy as children in horror films and TV series. What's scarier? Children who are being manipulated by something — or someone — unknown, that is. It's doubtful that The Exorcist would have been as effective had Regan (Linda Blair) been an adult, or Sinister as seriously messed up as it is if Bughuul did his dirty work through senior citizens. This brings us to The Whispers, a forgotten, 13-part sci-fi horror series that premiered on ABC in 2015 from executive producer Steven Spielberg, where children communicate with an entity known only as Drill, who promises them rewards if they play his "games," resulting in a series of incidents that seemingly have no connection… until they do. Eleven years later, its creepy premise still makes an ordinary childhood friendship feel like a threat.

According to recent reports, the Whispers opens with a playful scene, as children in a yard run through sprinklers, blow bubbles, and do what kids do. That is, except Harper (Abby Ryder Fortson), who's off to the side, talking to someone we can only assume is an imaginary friend she's named Drill. Her mother, Amanda (Autumn Reeser), calls her in, much to Harper's chagrin. She hasn't learned all the rules for the game Drill wants her to play yet.

What the game is, no one knows, but it involves Harper collecting tools and going up into the treehouse, where she's not supposed to be alone. Amanda storms out, but Harper won't come down, claiming that it's part of the game, and Drill says that Amanda is now "it." Amanda climbs up, walks to an "X" drawn on the floor, and promptly crashes through, hitting the ground, seriously injuring her and sending her into a coma.

It's the opening salvo in a battle against an unknown entity, one that may be supernatural or even alien in nature, and one that picks and chooses the children it "whispers" to further its own agenda. It's up to Special Agent Claire Bennigan (Lily Rabe), an FBI child specialist, and Wes Lawrence (Barry Sloane), a high-ranking Defense Department operative, to find out who or what Drill is, why he's targeting children for his games, and what his endgame could be.

Sources indicate that it takes on an increased urgency for each of them, given they all have their own children. Additionally, Claire's husband, U.S. Air Force pilot Captain Sean Bennigan (Milo Ventimiglia), who was thought to have died in a plane crash, is part of Drill's game. And Drill's always one step ahead.

The Whispers seamlessly blends sci-fi and horror with an unsettling eeriness, deepening and building the mystery with an underlying, ever-increasing anxiety. (And yes, it's thanks to those creepy kids.) Each of the young actors in primary roles — Fortson, Kyle Harrison Breitkopf, Kylie Rogers, and Kayden Magnuson — is brilliant, playing innocents unaware (maybe) of the consequences of playing Drill's games (Magnuson is particularly chilling in the finale). The adult cast, too, is strong. Ventimiglia is the strongest of the adult cast, playing what is essentially two different characters in the first and second half of the season.

The Whispers also bears an undeniable mark of its executive producer: the exploration of the adult/child dynamic. The children listen to Drill and are willing to do his bidding because he listens to them, and the adults in their lives don't. From Hook to The Fabelmans to E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial, there's a repeated theme of the disconnect between adults and children in Spielberg's works. Adults are absent, oblivious, and even antagonistic, and that's no different in The Whispers. The children are told that they're not allowed to talk to their imaginary friend. They leave their homes — despite so-called adult supervision — to carry out Drill's instructions in perilous ways.

Industry observers note that while most Spielberg fare has adults learning to pay more attention to their children, The Whispers ends on a life lesson, faced with the consequences of adults not paying attention until it's too late. It begs the question: who is the real danger, Drill or the parents? It's actually Drill who makes the argument for the latter, saying: "If parents paid more attention to them, I wouldn't have been able to [corrupt them]. But they're always alone, watching TV, playing video games. So, who's really corrupting the children, Claire?".

Industry observers note that but it's a question that would go unanswered, along with a host of others, with ABC pulling the plug on The Whispers after one season that ends on a major, unresolved cliffhanger. Don't let that stop you: The Whispers is the perfect weekend binge that keeps the viewer engaged from start to finish, and is a thrilling and eerie ride worth taking. Unless your child starts talking to an imaginary friend.

The Whispers is available to buy digitally on Amazon in the U.S.; a Prime subscription does not include it.

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

Sources indicate that “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang noted in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the organization, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

In a recent development, even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the tech giant to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

In a recent development, what do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

It has been revealed that ““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a significant improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

According to recent reports, starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

Sources indicate that if you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:.

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $30 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original debuted all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $39.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails between $59.99 and $69.99 for a physical copy, but Nintendo is selling it for $39.99 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

In a recent development, nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo confirmed a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It has been revealed that it depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 Latest York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.].

It has been revealed that paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026 ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker.

Industry observers note that last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy Newly introduced York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its Newly introduced York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

It has been revealed that the result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

According to recent reports, “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the Latest York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

Having originally rolled out in March 1996, the Resident Evil franchise is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, and with twelve mainline titles and over sixty total releases ranging from mobile, spin-offs, and remakes, it is safe to say that the Capcom horror franchise is one of the best.

Most recently, Resident Evil Requiem took 2026 by storm, and here at Screen Rant, our very own Chris Carter awarded the most recent mainline installment an almost perfect 9/10, with his review reading:.

Still, playing as two characters that are this starkly different from each other is an experiment that paid off, and worked out far better than it did with Resident Evil 6. Capcom has thrills down to a science at this point, and Resident Evil Requiem delivers. Long-time fans are going to get more out of this entry than the previous two, and the development team seems to have mastered the first-person perspective. Here's hoping a VR mode comes eventually.

In a recent development, now, nine months later and Resident Evil is back in the spotlight after some remakes made their way to the Nintendo Switch 2 back in October. Courtesy of Capcom, three modern Resident Evil remakes arrived digitally on 16 October with 55.9GB worth of gameplay to get stuck into. This includes: Resident Evil 2 Deluxe Edition, Resident Evil 3, and Resident Evil 4 Gold Edition.

Introducing a brand-fresh audience to the original titles, they are now available to purchase on the Nintendo eShop, but if you wish to get hold of them digitally, you will have to wait until January 2027. Even then, there has been no confirmation whether this will be a physical cartridge or a digital code. If recent releases *cough cough* Grand Theft Auto VI *cough cough* is anything to go by, then I would not get your hopes up.

It has been revealed that the good news here is that the Switch 2 remakes do not just feature the base game, but also include all of the DLC for each game. For example, Resident Evil 4 Gold Edition contains both the base game and its much-loved Separate Ways DLC.

However, we are not just heading to the past when it comes to Resident Evil, as the horror franchise is expected to continue with the launch of the Resident Evil - Code: Veronica remake which is expected to arrive some time in 2027. Yes, it may be another remake, but it is a much-needed one, as the initial release was way back in 2000. For now, it is the only known Resident Evil entry to right now be in development, and will take players back to Rockfort Island and follows the story of siblings, Claire and Chris, after the former is captured by the Umbrella Corporation.

So, if you wish to head back to where it all began with some classic Resident Evil entries, you can now download them all on the Nintendo eShop. However, if you wish to get your hands on their physical counterparts, you will have to wait until January 2027, and hope that it will include a physical cartridge and not just a measly download code.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the firm’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the firm’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:.

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

According to recent reports, as for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the organization’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, consumers can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

Sources indicate that VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:.

What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.
  • To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro.
  • Sources indicate that “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole upcoming task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026.

Sources indicate that “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a fresh idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

It has been revealed that to that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try newly introduced looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro noted. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

Recent findings suggest that hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro remarked. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

In a recent development, hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I promptly made a upcoming design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro stated. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

Industry observers note that during one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and stated, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro stated. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

Starting today, the Gemini app’s “tasks” feature, previously known as Spark, is now available for free users after requiring AI Pro in the past.

Above the prompt box on mobile (or below on the web), you’ll see “Chat” and “Task.” The first option is the existing chatbot, while the latter lets you “hand off even more tasks to Gemini.”.

With tasks, Google’s “goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.” Google shared use cases like:.

With today’s announcement, Google is emphasizing that “Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because [your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards] already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.”.

Behind the scenes, Gemini tasks work in your own “hardware-isolated virtual machine” that’s sandboxed and has protections against prompt injection, while leveraging Google Safe Browsing when browsing the web.

Other safety features include having you confirm purchases and asking “clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.”.

Powered by the latest Hydrogen model, free Gemini tasks are available in the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

  • According to recent reports, netflix has released hundreds of indicates over the years, and many were axed after the first season for reasons ranging from budget to low viewership.
  • Recent findings suggest that once Netflix customers watch five minutes of Blue Eye Samurai, they will wish they'd watched this show sooner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix has frequently proven that good things come in small packages when it comes to original television highlights. Some of them had short episode counts on purpose, while others were canceled too soon. The number of episodes doesn't define a television show's quality, but it can play a role in how impactful the series is for audiences.

According to recent reports, netflix has released hundreds of indicates over the years, and many were axed after the first season for reasons ranging from budget to low viewership. However, the streaming platform has a pattern of releasing critically acclaimed miniseries, and low-episode-count shows have been turning into cult classics. With that in mind, here is our list of the greatest Netflix shows with fewer than 30 episodes that are available to stream right now.

Recent findings suggest that once Netflix customers watch five minutes of Blue Eye Samurai, they will wish they'd watched this show sooner. The show follows Mizu (Maya Erskine), a mixed-race Japanese warrior who is seeking vengeance against the men who may be responsible for her birth. She does all this disguised as a boy, and adjusts to being accompanied by Ringo (Masi Oka), and later teaming up with Taigen (Darren Barnet).

What makes one of the greatest samurai TV shows refreshing is the decision to redefine gender stereotypes, even though the characters don't know this is happening. Mizu's personal story is painful to take in, but it's her history that gives her the strength to fight and destroy the opponents who underestimate her. All the voice actors were phenomenal at turning up the hype, which will grow following the Season 2 premiere, and continue to build in the months leading up to the third and final season.

Sources indicate that although this show lasted only two seasons, Russian Doll has aged like fine wine thanks to the heart and unique humor put into it. The series follows Nadia Vulvokov (Natasha Lyonne), a software engineer who keeps dying and reliving her 36th birthday party in an ongoing time loop. The belief that she is hallucinating in a nightmare takes a shocking turn when she meets Alan Zaveri (Charlie Barnett), who, like her, is living in a time loop, and dying all the time.

It has been revealed that lyonne, who is one of the show's co-creators, is known for applying humor so naturally to any character she portrays, even in serious films or television shows. Her performance in Russian Doll was no different; and the combination of her personality with Nadia's made viewers see the connection the actress shares with Nadia, while watching her character learn about life and undergoing personal growth. Although Russian Doll may have become a show audiences have never heard of, they won't forget it once they watch one of its 15 episodes on Netflix.

Sources indicate that derry Girls was already one of the best dark comedy TV reveals of all time, and aired on Channel 4 in the United Kingdom before it became available to stream internationally on Netflix. The show focuses on the lives of Erin Quinn (Saoirse-Monica Jackson), Orla McCool (Louisa Harland), Claire Devlin (Nicola Coughlan), Michelle Mallon (Jamie-Lee O'Donnell), and James Maguire (Dylan Llewellyn), in the 1990s during Ireland's political conflict, The Troubles. The teenagers go through typical, coming-of-age situations in school and with their parents, but as time goes on, they begin to pay closer attention to the political situation around them.

Recent findings suggest that it may be hard to imagine that a dark comedy is also one of the most educational representations of The Troubles in the eyes of adolescents and adults. Every actor portrayed reality with grace, and it was phenomenal to see the show's plots backed up by archive footage of things like news stories, and a speech delivered by then-President Bill Clinton in Derry back in 1995. Although Derry Girls had enough popularity to last for years, series creator Lisa McGee always planned to end the show after Season 3, which makes it one of the best TV shows under 20 episodes.

In a recent development, this 10-episode miniseries is not only the greatest horror miniseries of all time, but it's also one that audiences may not want to watch alone in the dark. The Haunting of Hill House shows the terrifying story of the Crain family, and their experience living and eventually fleeing a haunted mansion in 1992, without the family matriarch. Years later, Stephen Crain (Michiel Huisman), Shirley Crain Harris (Elizabeth Reaser), Luke Crain (Oliver Jackson-Cohen), and Theodora "Theo" Crain (Kate Siegel) are estranged, but reunited following an increase of strange occurrences, including visions of their late sister, Eleanor "Nell" Crain Vance (Victoria Pedretti).

Every young and adult actor's performance is undeniably amazing, and their commitment to highlighting their characters’ trauma and coping mechanisms only makes the horror more real for viewers. Although the characters' experiences made this one of the scariest TV reveals of all time, it also made viewers have a new appreciation for family members, especially their parents and siblings. Pedretti and Jackson-Cohen are among the multiple actors who returned to play different characters in the follow-up miniseries, The Haunting of Bly Manor, which is also considered one of the best horror miniseries.

Baby Reindeer is full of mind-blowing plot twists that fans love to keep up with. The show begins with Donny Dunn (Richard Gadd) attempting to file a police report after claiming he was being stalked by Martha Scott (Jessica Gunning), a lawyer who is no stranger to criminal mischief. Their encounters go from harmless to chilling, and her harassment worsens to the point where Donny is no longer the only victim in her latest round of stalking behavior. Although Martha's actions are hair-raising, they were needed for Donny to begin facing his fears, and accept who he is.

Industry observers note that gadd and Gunning's chemistry was undeniable in the most creepy way possible. The actors' passion in their performances proved to viewers that they were the only stars who could play these roles, and it was easy to feel Martha's anger and Donny's intimidation just by looking at their faces in all seven episodes. Their performances were only part of the reason why this show is one of the best miniseries of the 2020s, and they each took home a Golden Globe Award to prove it.

It has been revealed that mindhunter will always be a canceled crime show worth watching that deserves more than two seasons. Based on the true-crime book Mindhunter: Inside the FBI's Elite Serial Crime Unit, the show revolves around FBI agents, Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany), who, along with Wendy Carr (Anna Torv), interview and seek information from serial killers about their crimes and motivations, and apply that information to future cases. Set in the '70s and early '80s, viewers get an inside look into the early years of the Behavioral Science Unit, which is known for helping law enforcement with brutal crimes, and preventing terrorism.

Groff did not waste any time creating the personality of a no-nonsense agent seeking ways to improve the FBI. It was a 180 from his Glee character, Jesse St. James, and it highlighted viewers that Groff can go outside his comfort zone. The show could've had the potential to become an Emmy and Golden Globe Award winner if it hadn't been canceled, but it will always be one of the darkest TV dramas of the last 10 years.

Beth Harmon (Anya Taylor-Joy) portrays a chess player out for blood in this seven-episode miniseries. The Queen's Gambit explores Beth's journey to reach her dream of becoming a grandmaster, all while battling addiction and overcoming family drama in her birth and adoptive families. Her journey takes her all over the world with her adoptive mother, Alma Wheatley (Marielle Heller), and helps her form bonds with multiple chess players, including D.L. Townes (Jacob Fortune-Loyd), Harry Beltik (Harry Melling), and Benny Watts (Thomas Brodie-Sangster).

Taylor-Joy found the right balance between determination and intensity in her performance, and made it clear to viewers that she was the only person who could accurately portray the perfection-seeking Beth. Her character only wanted perfection, and when that didn't happen, a glimpse of the depression she hid from the world surfaced. Taylor-Joy revealed audiences that even a perfect person is haunted by something, and her Golden Globe-winning performance helped make The Queen's Gambit one of the greatest Netflix miniseries of all time.

This German-language show is raw, complex, and one of the best sci-fi mystery shows of all time. Dark is set in Winden, a small town startled by the disappearance of two children, leaving families to suffer the collateral damage that comes of it. Jonas Kahnwad (Louis Hofmann), a teenager reeling over the loss of his father, soon discovers the disappearances, and other town secrets, are connected to a time-travel loop.

In a recent development, unlike some sci-fi series, Dark puts characters front and center, and factors in their emotions when exploring the time traveling and supernatural aspects of the show. Audiences may still be surprised to learn it's one of the best Netflix shows with three seasons, especially since the complexity seems too much to fit into only 26 episodes. Everything came together by the end of the series, and while some viewers may now be afraid to start families, they were able to witness a satisfying ending that concluded all character arcs.

Sources indicate that when They See Us is not only one of the saddest miniseries of all time, it's also based on the true story of the 1989 Central Park jogger case. The first two episodes center around the arrests of Kevin Richardson (Asante Blackk), Antron McCray (Caleel Harris), Yusef Salaam (Ethan Herisse), Raymond Santana (Marquis Rodriguez), and Korey Wise (Jharrel Jerome), for the assault and rape of Trisha Meili (Alexandra Templer), and the events leading up to their confessions and convictions. The final two episodes show the difficulty of some of these men returning to society, Wise's treatment in prison, and the truth behind what happened to Trisha in Central Park.

According to recent reports, every actor's facial expressions throughout the miniseries represented the pain the Exonerated Five and their families felt during the events leading up to their exoneration. However, Jerome's outstanding performance shook audiences to their core, and the Emmy Award-winning actor portrayed the fear Korey may have had in prison beautifully. The Central Park jogger case has become an example of racial profiling and discrimination in the media and legal system, and When They See Us provides viewers with a detailed explanation as to why.

Recent findings suggest that adolescence is a miniseries that's a 10/10 masterpiece that is both brilliant and terrifying. The four-episode show centers around Jamie Miller (Owen Cooper), a 13-year-old boy accused of brutally murdering a classmate. His arrest leads to shocking details about the events before and after the crime, as well as the pain his family endures from everyone who is furious at Jamie.

Miller's performance was unforgettably brilliant, and it's still hard to believe that this was his debut acting role, even a year after the miniseries premiered. It's usually difficult for an adult actor to give audiences chills for their antagonistic performance on a television show, but Miller had no problem doing so during the third and best Adolescence episode. Besides Miller, Stephen Graham and Erin Doherty were phenomenal in portraying the vulnerability and emotions behind each character, and their performances led to the trio each winning an Emmy and a Golden Globe Award.

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

It has been revealed that there was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Industry observers note that chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in Fresh York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

The original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

John Wick: Chapter 4 concluded with the death of the titular character, thus appearing to put an end to its epic saga. However, as phenomenal an ending as it was, there's clearly a lot more juice left in the proverbial engine, as future John Wick installments have been greenlit and confirmed to be in production. Keanu Reeves is also set to play John Wick three more times across different entries, so even the iconic actor is still very much attached to the series.

Among all of the upcoming John Wick projects is a brand-upcoming prequel release that is set to recount the events leading up to both the Impossible Task and the first film. This is a completely different release from the upcoming John Wick prequel movie, which was recently confirmed to still be in production with Keanu Reeves. Rather, this John Wick prequel will allow fans to get right into the action themselves and experience John Wick's penchant for gun fu up close and personal.

The Untitled John Wick Game is an upcoming video game that is set to tell the story of John Wick prior to the Impossible Task. Developed by Saber Interactive (the same folks behind the incredible Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2) in collaboration with Lionsgate and John Wick director Chad Stahelski, the Untitled John Wick Game is going to be the most ambitious adaptation of the series yet, following in the footsteps of the far humbler, yet nevertheless excellent indie, John Wick: Hex.

Untitled John Wick Game aims to faithfully recreate the experience of watching the film, albeit in video game form, offering a robust gun-fu combat system that is paired with stylized camera angles, explosive driving set pieces, and cinematic storytelling. While the reveal trailer tells us little of the full experience, it does give fans a firm idea of the tone and type of gameplay style Saber Interactive is aiming for, as well as the familiar, and not so familiar, faces we can expect to see pop up during the story.

It has been revealed that on the game's official website, Saber Interactive describes it as the "ultimate John Wick gaming experience that fans have been waiting for." It isn't hard to see how that could be true, especially with the stunning, near-photorealistic visuals (that still maintain the neon-soaked style of the original films) and intense combat animations. It's likely that the Untitled John Wick Game will be akin to the recent James Bond game, 007: First Light, or perhaps even Sifu, as a linear, action-focused title interspersed with cinematic cutscenes or set pieces.

So far, we know very little about the Untitled John Wick Game, something that should be evident from the lack of a confirmed title. It was confirmed back in February 2026, so it has been quite a while since Saber Interactive showed us anything. This could mean that more will be shown in the coming months, perhaps even during the Game Awards, although that is pure speculation. Regardless, it is exciting that fans are finally getting a big-budget John Wick video game, and one from a studio with a proven track record of working with existing IP.

How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • Sources indicate that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be crucial for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

Sources indicate that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be crucial for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

Industry observers note that “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado remarked. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

Recent findings suggest that for Crawford, the major lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

Industry observers note that “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

In a recent development, still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

Industry observers note that “Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado mentioned. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford mentioned, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other significant studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.
