’The Mummy’s’ Best Line Is Still the Greatest Quote in Franchise History

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Mummy movies are a celebrated blend of action, adventure, and comedy that still remain popular — and immensely quotable —decades after the first film’s 1999 release.
  • Sources indicate that for the uninitiated, 1999’s The Mummy follows Evelyn, a librarian and aspiring Egyptologist who, along with her brother Jonathan (John Hannah), free adventurer Rick O’Connell from prison so that he can help them find a mythical location, where they accidentally awaken the cursed high priest Imhotep.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s this difference in worldviews that leads to the film’s best line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Mummy movies are a celebrated blend of action, adventure, and comedy that still remain popular — and immensely quotable —decades after the first film’s 1999 release. There are many memorable lines that fans of the trilogy will quote to each other, from the swashbuckling Rick O’Connell (Brendan Fraser) declaring: “I only gamble with my life, never my money,” or Dr. Bey (Erick Avari) despairing: “When Rameses destroyed Syria, that was an accident. You are a catastrophe!” However, one quote from the original movie stands out as the greatest in the whole series. Spoken by Evelyn Carnahan (Rachel Weisz), it defines exactly why, with the fourth movie on the horizon, we hold the world of these films so close to our hearts.

Sources indicate that for the uninitiated, 1999’s The Mummy follows Evelyn, a librarian and aspiring Egyptologist who, along with her brother Jonathan (John Hannah), free adventurer Rick O’Connell from prison so that he can help them find a mythical location, where they accidentally awaken the cursed high priest Imhotep. Along with a series of delightful action sequences, the film focuses on the clash of personalities between bookworm Evelyn and cavalier treasure hunter Rick.

Recent findings suggest that it’s this difference in worldviews that leads to the film’s best line. In a drunken moment beside a campfire, Evelyn declares: “I may not be an explorer, or an adventurer, or a treasure-seeker, or a gunfighter, Mr. O’Connell, but I am proud of what I am.” Amused, Rick asks: “And what is that?”, before Evelyn looks to the middle distance, smiles, and replies: “I... am a librarian.” It’s a moment of comedy, but one that also sums up the charming relationship at the center of this film and the 2001 sequel, The Mummy Returns. Weisz was unavailable for the 2008 third movie, The Mummy: The Tomb of the Dragon Emperor, replaced by Maria Bello, but her return for the fourth film, at the moment in production, was celebrated by fans precisely because of the dynamic that this speech encapsulates.

The Mummy movies have broadly the same appeal as the Indiana Jones franchise, with exotic locations, ancient mysteries, and colorful characters populating a rich and entertaining world. While they may attract similar audiences, The Mummy differentiated itself from the classic Steven Spielberg franchise by making two characters the focus, rather than a single adventurer with a secondary character who serves as a potential love interest. The Mummy doesn’t work without Evelyn and Rick bantering, as well as using their very different skills in order to achieve their goals. Evelyn’s speech, while funny, highlights how crucial that dynamic is to the story.

Rick is strong, courageous, and charismatic, getting the group out of more than one dangerous moment over the course of the movies. However, it takes more than his heroism to get the job done. Evelyn’s brains, instincts, and curiosity are vital to their discovering hidden wonders, making her as important to the movie as her future husband. She is not a sidekick, or a damsel in distress, but an equal partner in an on-screen coupling that made Hollywood magic. There’s no Rick without Evelyn, giving her every right to cherish her love of knowledge.

In a recent development, the fourth movie in the franchise, The Mummy: Book of the Dead, is currently filming for a planned 2027 release. The first images of Weisz in costume as Evelyn recently emerged online, with fans delighted to see her stylish return to the beloved role. The popularity of the leak stems from fans who grew up with the movies acknowledging her as a vital part of the franchise, someone that audiences are keen to see as an older woman, a mother, still tearing across the world in search of adventure.

Sources indicate that many movies have had long-awaited sequels in recent years – Gladiator and Beetlejuice both got follow-ups in 2024, while fellow globe-trotter Indiana Jones came back for one last mission in 2023’s The Dial of Destiny. By the time the fourth Mummy film arrives, it will have been 17 years since the last time we saw an entry in the saga, and 26 since we saw Weisz play Evelyn. So why are fans so excited to see her back? Because, in all that time, her wit and fearlessness have been replayed on home video and streaming services for an entire generation. She is a character that endured because of her nerdiness, not in spite of it. We love this librarian and celebrate her return.

In a recent development, the Mummy has been adapted twice since this action-adventure trilogy was released: in 2017 as a Tom Cruise blockbuster, and in 2026 with Lee Cronin’s The Mummy. Both were poorly received, both critically and by theater audiences, and perhaps the reason for that is the affection with which Evelyn and Rick are held in the hearts of movie fans. Maybe you don’t need elevated scares or plane crash sequences to make a hit. Perhaps you just need a librarian.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-announced third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a Newly introduced Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest newly introduced director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

“I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really quickly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” mentioned Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

“It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

It has been revealed that “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” remarked Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how quickly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” remarked Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Sources indicate that directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

According to recent reports, what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly states he fell short in “Obsession.”.

“Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

Breaking: 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • Recent findings suggest that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

Recent findings suggest that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

According to recent reports, next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, enhancement the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that netflix's upcoming 4-part crime thriller is trending #2 worldwide, offering a gripping one-night binge inspired by a disturbing real-life murder case. After only a few days on the platform, this new Netflix series has become an overnight streaming sensation across the globe and is even the top trending show in multiple countries at the time of writing. Even with multiple exciting new reveals to binge on Netflix this weekend, such as The Altruists and Murder in Galicia, this 4-part crime thriller is rapidly proving that it belongs among the very best.

In a recent development, the Law of Beasts just landed on Netflix on Wednesday, November 18, and is aiming for the streamer's #1 viewership spot this weekend, which it will have to dethrone the viral psychological horror series The Body to accomplish. With 4 sharply paced episodes and a gripping story based on historically significant events, this is the ultimate one-night binge on Netflix this weekend, especially for fans of movie-length series and true crime content. If you're stuck deciding what to watch on Netflix right now, The Law of Beasts is a safe streaming bet.

According to recent reports, the Law of Beasts is based on real-life events and an elaborate moral dilemma with Poland's judicial system that permanently changed the nation's laws regarding incarcerated persons, especially violent criminals. The Beast Law was put into effect in January 2014, allowing courts to legally send convicts to psychiatric institutions after completing court-ordered federal prison sentences. The law was designed to prevent criminals still deemed dangerous to society from reintegration, which challenged Poland's established constitutional rights given to all citizens. The series is based on the impending release of a serial child murderer who killed four boys between the ages of 11 and 13.

Sources indicate that the latest Netflix series is told between two overlapping timelines in 1988 and 2014, which mark the beginning and end of a child murderer, Mariusz Trynkiewicz's, 25-year prison sentence. Originally sentenced to the death penalty, Trynkiewicz received an amnesty in 1989 and received a reduced sentence, which allowed the possibility of his release. As that release date neared in 2013, there was a public outcry in Poland that called for further judicial action to be taken. This is how the Beast Law was conceived and implemented, forcing Trynkiewicz to be transferred to a psych hospital specifically for convicted felons. The law that still exists in Poland to this day.

In a recent development, the two protagonists of Netflix's upcoming The Law of Beasts series are Anna Bersz, played by Agnieszka Grochowska, and Agnieszka Grabska, played by Agnieszka Żulewska. Both characters are fictional and not based on real persons involved with the actual Trynkiewicz case, invented purely as narrative devices for the Netflix series. Anna is a police detective who led the investigation into Trynkiewicz in 1988 and became a government official by 2014, whose interest lies primarily in public safety. Agnieszka is a psychiatrist who is assigned to examine Trynkiewicz's mental state, siding with psychological analysis and reasoning, and is a believer in protecting individual rights.

Anna and Agnieszka are lifelong friends who come into great conflict over the release of Trynkiewicz, serving as two opposite ends of the moral and legal spectrum regarding the Beast Law. Anna thinks in black-and-white terms of good and evil, while Agnieszka understands psychological complexities that determine degrees of criminal responsibility. Even though they are fictional characters, they embody the central conflict within the real-life philosophical conundrum regarding Trynkiewicz.

It has been revealed that ultimately, with the Beast Law put into law, it's already clear whose perspective changed Poland's history. The real-life Trynkiewicz was sent to a psych hospital/federal prison hybrid before being sent back to prison in 2015 for possession of child pornography. He died in custody in 2025. For a fascinating and chilling 4-part binge, you can't beat The Law of Beasts on Netflix this weekend.

#51358. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (851 w)

Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • In a recent development, perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

In a recent development, perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

Industry observers note that if you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an glitch with the Duo itself.

Industry observers note that I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

Recent findings suggest that I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for highlights and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Recent findings suggest that multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

It has been revealed that after a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

Industry observers note that I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

It has been revealed that I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

It has been revealed that the iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique newly introduced iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#51356. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2029 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • In a recent development, to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

In a recent development, to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

According to recent reports, it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Recent findings suggest that horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

According to recent reports, I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

It has been revealed that there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

Recent findings suggest that I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

Sources indicate that the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

Sources indicate that A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

#51355. How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • Industry observers note that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • According to recent reports, when he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Industry observers note that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

According to recent reports, when he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation A ‘Home Alone’ Legacyquel with Macaulay Culkin in Early Development with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg.

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

It has been revealed that so instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

Sources indicate that at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he mentioned. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

It has been revealed that how’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” said Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

According to recent reports, of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he remarked. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he said. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he stated. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he remarked, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

According to recent reports, airPods got a variety of newly introduced features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods people thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:.

Industry observers note that airPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV reveals and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:.

It has been revealed that the setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

According to recent reports, once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym.

For most AirPods consumers, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

It has been revealed that airPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the latest Siri. It will let customers do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:.

Industry observers note that earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of latest AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that 9-1-1 continues to go in circles with Buck's character in Season 10, making him regress to the point of impulsively giving up the child he chose to foster instead of actually working through his trauma and self-worth problems.
  • It has been revealed that after spending pretty much all of his non-work screen time this season supporting Buck, Eddie got to make a bold move in last week's episode when he chose to foster Theo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for 9-1-1 Season 10, Episode 6.9-1-1 is just six episodes into its tenth season, but the show already just aired its mid-season finale. Any network procedural fan knows it's standard for each main character to get a couple solo storylines during a shorter half-season like this, except for the show's leads – which, since the beginning of 9-1-1, were Athena (Angela Bassett) and Bobby (Peter Krause). Since Bobby's death, Athena has been 9-1-1's main lead, while the other characters each get a significant storyline every few episodes. Buck (Oliver Stark), however, has been getting more storylines than everyone else this season.

It has been revealed that 9-1-1 continues to go in circles with Buck's character in Season 10, making him regress to the point of impulsively giving up the child he chose to foster instead of actually working through his trauma and self-worth problems. Five episodes have been dedicated to the Theo (Lincoln and Theodore Sykes) storyline this season, and every Buck and Eddie (Ryan Guzman) storyline this season has been about Theo. The latter wouldn't necessarily be a problem, except that 9-1-1 is still giving Buck way too much focus without real growth, while unfairly relegating Eddie to the supporting role.

It has been revealed that after spending pretty much all of his non-work screen time this season supporting Buck, Eddie got to make a bold move in last week's episode when he chose to foster Theo. Even knowing that Buck would take this as a personal slight, Eddie prioritized the needs of Theo over the second most important relationship in his life – barring that with Christopher (Gavin McHugh), who cares deeply about Theo and even wrote Buck an angry letter for giving him up. 9-1-1 set up something compelling here, where viewers could see how Eddie adjusted to raising a second child, and how he's been feeling about this entire situation. This was the perfect opportunity to get a rare insight into Eddie's emotions, and to see the pain that Buck's cruel remarks caused him.

Instead, Eddie only gets a little bit of focus in the mid-season finale. 9-1-1 finally delivers the long-anticipated first scene between Eddie and Maddie (Jennifer Love Hewitt), but the whole scene sees Maddie treating Eddie coldly and accusing him of fostering Theo to teach Buck a lesson. Maddie hasn't been afraid to call Buck out in the past, like when he hurt Eddie's ankle in "Buck, Bothered and Bewildered." Here, though, she takes his side when Eddie isn't even acting against him, and everyone from the 118 except for Ravi (Anirudh Pisharody) also backs Buck up. Eddie doesn't get to talk about his feelings or his latest role as a foster parent at all, and he instead oddly emphasizes the apparent importance of Buck's role as Theo's biological parent.

The Buck and Eddie pairing became so beloved by fans because of their deep friendship and care for each other. They always supported each other through the toughest moments and showed up for each other – until now. Eddie tried to give Buck helpful and honest advice earlier this season, but Buck just lashed out at him. Eddie later stepped up and did something really thoughtful to help both Buck and Theo, and Buck blew up at him again. Instead of having each other's backs like they promised they would before they even became friends, Eddie's been consistently monitoring Buck's back, while Buck can't so much as be bothered to turn around and look at him. Everyone this season is coddling Buck except for Eddie, but Eddie's still been exceptionally gentle with him, refusing to even accept his lackluster apology without also unfairly blaming himself.

Becoming a foster parent has the potential to be an amazing storyline for Eddie, but not in the way 9-1-1 is right now setting it up, where Eddie is just a stand-in parent for Theo until Buck is ready to take him back. 9-1-1 should focus on Eddie's journey of parenting a second child, as well as the memories that this will inevitably bring up for him from Christopher's childhood. Then, either Theo needs to stay with Eddie, or Buck and Eddie need to find a solution that works for them – because it would do Eddie a tremendous disservice to have him simply give Theo back to Buck after choosing to parent him. Considering the show has neglected Eddie's storyline all season, it's about time that he gets something more than just the crumbs of a storyline from Buck.

Industry observers note that 9-1-1 will return to ABC on Thursday, January 7 at 8:00 P.M. EST.

Disney's 6-Part Superhero Series Is The Perfect Mix Of Sci-Fi & Fantasy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since science fiction and fantasy are at odds, it can be tough to blend the two.
  • Star Wars has the wizards and dragons of a classic fantasy tale and the faster-than-light space travel of a sci-fi epic, but you’d call it more of a space fantasy than a blend of fantasy and sci-fi.
  • Industry observers note that in the summer of 2025, Disney+ released the millionth streaming show set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since science fiction and fantasy are at odds, it can be tough to blend the two. Sci-fi is supposed to be rooted in some kind of logic — an A.I. becomes sentient, an alien visitor comes to Earth, an astronaut gets stranded in space with no fuel, etc. — but fantasy is just made-up escapism where sorcerers fight fire-breathing dragons and magic systems control the universe.

Star Wars has the wizards and dragons of a classic fantasy tale and the faster-than-light space travel of a sci-fi epic, but you’d call it more of a space fantasy than a blend of fantasy and sci-fi. Shows like Loki and Stranger Things and The X-Files all have elements of both sci-fi and fantasy, but end up falling more one way than the other. Loki’s time-traveling cops are hard sci-fi, The X-Files’ FBI investigations into UFO sightings are hard sci-fi, and Stranger Things’ dark dimension full of monsters feels a lot more fantasy than sci-fi (although there is a lot of Altered States thrown in there).

Industry observers note that in the summer of 2025, Disney+ released the millionth streaming show set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Ironheart took Riri Williams, the precocious robotics student we met in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever, and sent her into a world of magic and sorcery, where her futuristic tech can’t always save her.

In a recent development, in the years since Avengers: Endgame, Marvel Studios has been telling story after story setting up the next generation of Avengers to succeed the O.G.s. Black Widow was all about Yelena Belova taking over for her sister Natasha Romanoff; The Falcon and the Winter Soldier was all about Sam Wilson taking on Steve Rogers’ mantle as Captain America; Hawkeye was all about Kate Bishop taking the reins from Clint Barton; The Marvels was all about Kamala Khan looking up to Carol Danvers.

Recent findings suggest that when Ironheart premiered, it seemed like another tired passing-the-torch narrative. Riri would build her own suit of armor and succeed Tony Stark as the iron-themed superhero of the Avengers. But as the series went on, it rapidly differentiated itself from Tony’s story by introducing a hefty dose of magic.

Industry observers note that riri’s power-armored vigilante crusade brings her to the attention of a local street gang led by “The Hood,” a sorcerer who uses his powers for evil. Ironheart is essentially a clash between science and magic, as Riri and the Hood keep trying to one-up each other, Riri with high-tech weapons and the Hood with nefarious sleight-of-hand. The series even introduced us to Marvel’s Devil, Mephisto, which brought out Riri’s unseen dark side in the shocking final episode.

Sources indicate that when Ironheart was declared, there was a valid concern that it would just be Iron Man 2.0. But the magical elements ensured that it had a feel of its own.

While reveals like Secret Invasion and What If...? and The Falcon and the Winter Soldier all deserve the complaints levied at them, Ironheart remains one of the MCU’s most underrated shows. The fan base treats Ironheart like it’s Secret Invasion when they should be treating it like it’s WandaVision. A lot of the MCU’s Disney+ shows feel like movie stories stretched to TV length, but Ironheart is genuinely engaging from start to finish. It hooks you with fascinating characters early on, then spends the next six episodes building to a jaw-dropping payoff.

In a recent development, ironheart has all the comic book spectacle you’ve come to expect from a Marvel show, but it touches on some deeper emotional substance, too. Riri’s tech brings her best friend back from the dead and digitally replicates their consciousness, paving the way for arguably an even more profound and moving exploration of grief than WandaVision itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’ How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation.

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

Sources indicate that “When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

Tech Report: Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a fresh filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the firm complies.
  • As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.
  • According to recent reports, apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a fresh filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the firm complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

According to recent reports, apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

According to recent reports, at the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a fresh filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic indicates Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”.

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”.

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a fresh order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a fresh report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a newly introduced Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

It has been revealed that apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That stated, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone customers surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was revealed, but before it rolled out, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level.
  • “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said.
  • In a recent development, trump mentioned Georgia and Fresh Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

In a recent development, trump mentioned Georgia and Fresh Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he stated, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Industry observers note that trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors confirmed more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he mentioned, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she said in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

According to recent reports, A floor vote has yet to be confirmed, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

According to recent reports, for crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s fresh Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff remarked.
