#51340. 10 Thriller Books That Hooked Me From the Opening Chapter

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2312 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Collider ↗ Open Full Page

10 Thriller Books That Hooked Me From the Opening Chapter

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that at any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention.
  • He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.
  • Some thriller writers seem terrified you'll put their book down, so they throw everything at you: a murder on page one and an abduction on page three, all while a massive conspiracy begins to unravel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

Some thriller writers seem terrified you'll put their book down, so they throw everything at you: a murder on page one and an abduction on page three, all while a massive conspiracy begins to unravel. And that’s all before introducing who’s involved. Eventful, sure, but there's something almost desperate about all that hoopla. It’s as if the writer's afraid one quiet page will send readers straight back to their phones.

Recent findings suggest that the best thriller writers have a little more faith in their stories. They're in no great hurry to show their hand, allowing the reader to become acquainted with a character worth following. Of course, there's nothing wrong with opening on a murder or throwing somebody into immediate danger, but the excitement alone can only take a story so far. What matters is that the writer gives us time to find our footing, to become familiar with the world we're entering and curious about what lies beyond it. By the end of that first chapter, we might have little idea where the story is headed, but we're more than happy to go along for the ride.

A woman burning her father’s corpse in the garden is a shocking way to start a novel, but Liz Nugent somehow makes it relatable in the opening pages of Strange Sally Diamond. Sally's father constantly joked that she should put him out with the trash when he died, so she does. Yet the way she recounts it, with the practicality of someone listing yet another household chore, you understand it. It's an absurd explanation, but Nugent delivers it so matter-of-factly that you begin to appreciate Sally's reasoning.

Industry observers note that that's what makes Nugent's introduction so effective: everyone else sees a 42-year-old woman who's done something appalling. The police have questions and turn Sally into a suspect. The neighbors are horrified and turn Sally into a monster. Sally is confused by all the hubbub. The reader is at an advantage here, having spent some time in Sally’s mind and following her peculiar train of thought, understanding her in a way nobody else does. The twists and the shock that follow only deepen that early compassion for a character that, on the surface, could be easily written off as psychotic.

According to recent reports, when you’ve got revolvers and shotguns pointed at your head, it usually spells endgame. Lee Child flips that script when introducing Jack Reacher in the opening of Killing Floor. Reacher is simply eating breakfast as four police officers descend on a Georgia diner. But he doesn’t fly off into action, doesn’t protest or attempt to escape: he quietly finishes his eggs and tucks five dollars under his plate. Reacher, in fact, is so composed that the police, all that firepower be damned, begin to look like the nervous ones.

It's a clever way to introduce a man who'll eventually become one of fiction's most formidable tough guys. Child could have staged some spectacular show of force, but instead he lets Reacher's observations do the work: he sizes up the officers and considers their tactics. And just when we're getting comfortable with the idea that Reacher is an innocent man caught in an unfortunate situation, Child drops a revelation: he hasn't killed anybody in this town. He hasn’t killed anyone in some time now. It’s the exclamation point to the chapter, a way of announcing the police may have arrested the wrong man, but he’s not a harmless one.

Sources indicate that sébastien Japrisot begins A Trap for Cinderella in just about the most non-thriller way possible: lulling the reader into a fairy tale. Mi and Do grew up together. The former is the ideal of the pair: beautiful and wealthy, the symbol of adoration for everyone around her. The latter is intelligent but poor, always getting the short end of the stick. But then Japrisot reveals that Do has invented this little fairy tale herself. She resents Mi, so she’s conveniently cast herself as Cinderella. It’s presented in such a way that we’ve no idea how much of what we've read is true.

That quiet beginning is a trap in itself as the novel takes a dark turn, with a fire at a villa on the French Riviera. The blaze leaves one woman dead and another so badly burned that she loses her memory. The survivor doesn't know whether she's Mi or Do, and the fire may have been deliberate, meaning she could be either the victim of an attempted murder or the person who planned it. Japrisot has already shown how easily a story can be twisted by the person telling it, and then allows his protagonist to reconstruct her entire life from what other people tell her.

Industry observers note that jean-Patrick Manchette’s opening to Fatale is a bit of a red herring. Almost the entire first chapter follows a man named Roucart on a hunting trip. We become overly familiar with his protruding belly and his deep regret at giving up smoking. It's the sort of attention you'd expect a writer to give someone we'll be following for the next few hundred pages. So when an attractive young woman appears in the woods, we assume she's wandered into Roucart's story. But she takes a shotgun off her shoulder and shoots him dead.

In a recent development, ultimately, it’s clever the way Manchette makes us almost as susceptible to this woman as Roucart. He was so enthralled by her appearance that he didn’t for a second recognize the danger. We, too, dismiss the danger, sliding past the fact that she just committed a cold-blooded murder because we're so intrigued by her composure, so curious about who she is. She arrives in a provincial town where the wealthy residents have plenty of dirty little secrets: they're a vain, greedy, thoroughly unpleasant lot, and watching her exploit their weaknesses becomes something of a pleasure. Before long, we're almost rooting for a woman we know is capable of murder.

Recent findings suggest that many a thriller makes revenge look easy, the only logical next step in the grieving process. It can look a lot different when you’re staring it square in the eye. That's the predicament Kōtarō Isaka gives a grieving father in the opening of Bullet Train. Yuichi Kimura boards a Japanese high-speed train intent on killing the teenager who pushed his six-year-old son off a rooftop. He's got the boy's seat number, a gun fitted with a silencer, and every reason to want him dead, but not the confidence. So when he sees his target, an innocent-looking schoolboy, he hesitates. The boy doesn't.

According to recent reports, and that's how Isaka introduces one of the novel's central ideas: Having a perfectly good reason to do something doesn't mean you're remotely able to pull it off. It's bad enough that Kimura's been outsmarted by a teenager, but worse, the boy finds his humiliation entertaining. And Isaka has plenty more fun at the expense of his characters as the train fills with professional killers, all convinced they know what they're doing. They're a dangerous bunch, sure, but for all their cleverness and carefully laid plans, they spend an awful lot of time making fools of themselves.

It has been revealed that jo Nesbø warps a symbol of winter wonderland into one of holiday horror in the opening pages of The Snowman. Sara Kvinesland meets her lover at his house, leaving her young son waiting in the car. She's nervous about someone catching them, so when her lover notices a face staring at them through the bedroom window, they both panic. But it's only a snowman, its pebble eyes fixed on the house. Except, snowmen don't build themselves — somebody went to the trouble of putting it right outside that window.

Sources indicate that nesbø lets that thought linger as Sara returns to her car, where her son is trembling behind locked doors, seeing something that's scared him half to death. Sara's got other things on her mind: she's worried about her affair and keeping up appearances. Her son can barely get her attention, even when he tells her they're going to die. And that's where Nesbø really gets under your skin: the boy knows something's wrong, but Sara, the one person who really should be listening, is too distracted to notice. There's no murder and no grisly discovery; just a snowman standing outside a house, and already we’re hooked.

According to recent reports, thirteen Hours opens at 5:36 a.m. with a woman running for her life. We don’t know why, or who’s chasing her, and we don’t find out. Deon Meyer leaves her, exhausted and terrified, desperate to escape the men who seem to want her dead. Meyer cuts to Detective Benny Griessel, who's being dragged out of bed by a phone call about a body outside a church. And the man’s got problems of his own: an estranged wife, another woman he slept with recently, and a 156-day desperate attempt to stay sober.

In a recent development, it's almost infuriating how casually Meyer abandons the woman, but that frustration only makes us more desperate to get back to her. Griessel, of course, hasn't the faintest idea she exists, and Meyer takes his time introducing the detective, giving us a man whose considerable professional experience is at odds with the mess he's made of his personal life. Each time Meyer takes us away from the woman, we're left worrying about what's happening to her while we're gone. And all the while, the clock keeps ticking, whether we're watching the woman running or not.

Recent findings suggest that an ex-con in a stolen car isn't exactly the person you'd entrust with an 11-year-old girl's safety, but Jordan Harper has us begging her to climb inside in the opening of She Rides Shotgun. You see, a prison gang has ordered the murder of Nate McClusky and his family, and he's racing to get his daughter Polly before the killers do. But Polly doesn't know: all she sees outside her school is a hulking man covered in tattoos and scars, a father she barely remembers and who's supposed to be behind bars.

Sources indicate that harper puts us in an uncomfortable position, knowing that the man Polly fears might be the only person capable of protecting her. And he plays with that contradiction throughout their uneasy reunion. Polly is painfully shy and bullied at school, carrying a teddy bear for comfort. Nate looks like he could frighten just about anybody. But as they're driving away, a police car passes, and Polly catches something on her father's face she'd never expected to see: fear. Now this intimidating man doesn't seem so invincible, and that's what makes the opening so compelling.

It's a familiar enough scene: a mother worried about a son who's out past his curfew. But Gillian McAllister takes that moment of parental anxiety to the extreme in the opening of Wrong Place Wrong Time. Jen is waiting up for her 18-year-old son, Todd, watching from the window of their Liverpool home as he finally comes down the street. She's relieved to see him, until a stranger approaches. Todd pulls a knife and stabs the man three times, and she hasn't the faintest idea why.

It's a horrible thing for a parent to witness, made worse by the realization that the child you've spent 18 years raising might be someone you don't know at all. McAllister gives Jen a chance to go back and find out. We watch as the clocks move backward through the rest of the novel, allowing her to revisit the days leading up to the murder. She knows who wielded the knife but not what drove him to it. This literal trip down memory lane allows her to scrutinize the years she's spent raising him, revisiting conversations and decisions she'd long since forgotten.

It has been revealed that it's easy to imagine what you'd do if someone broke into your house: grab the children, call the police, find something to defend yourself with. But Tracy Sierra makes those prepares laughably optimistic in the opening of Nightwatching, in which a mother hears footsteps on the stairs. She entertains just about every possibility until a stranger appears at the top of the stairs, so tall he nearly hits his head on the ceiling. Even then, she struggles to accept what's happening.

Sierra makes us endure every second of that hesitation, making the mental cycle of decisions seem visceral. She thinks of screaming, but doesn’t want the intruder to know she’s there. She thinks about moving, but doesn’t want to wake the children. All the while, her mind also keeps latching onto the most random of details, from the man's dry sneakers to the light falling across the landing. There's something convincing about the way she thinks, grasping at anything that might help her understand the situation while struggling to do something about it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud.
  • A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.
  • At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp owners running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Consumers can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot presently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning customers switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app enhancement.

There's little doubt at this point that the Prime Video adaptation of Fallout has done wonders for restoring some confidence in the franchise, and bringing in new fans from around the world. The unfortunate reality is that we still haven't had another single-player game in the series, and we're looking at quite a lengthy wait before one does debut.

What the show also did was bring back many memorable locations, factions and characters from the older games in the series, which really opened it up to nostalgia from long-time fans. Shady Sands is probably the most obvious example of this from the first season, with the arrival of Upcoming Vegas in the second continuing that trend to the benefit of the audience.

As we know with New Vegas, there are a ton of different factions who call the Mojave home, and one of the most iconic of those is about to be further immortalized thanks to a new physical release that would be a worthy centerpiece for any collection.

According to recent reports, over on the Sideshow website, you should be able to find the product page for the NCR Power Armor statue by Dark Horse Comics. Cast in durable PVC, it's a budget-friendly option that still manages to include a ton of details and little references for fans of the show.

The power armor itself is modeled on the suit that Maximus wears in his epic fight with the Deathclaws at the entrance to the New Vegas strip, and it sits on a base that's designed to look like a vault door, and includes the title in its recognizable font.

In sharing a little about the inspirations behind the statue, the manufacturer included the following description:.

"Dark Horse, in partnership with Amazon MGM Studios, continues our line of figures from the acclaimed Prime Video series, Fallout, this time pulling characters straight from the scenes of Season 2.

In a recent development, in the procession to rescue Lucy, The Ghoul takes Maximus and Thaddeus to an abandoned NCR safe house where they unearth the revered armor from the New California Republic. The NCR is a post-war federal republic-esque faction that values democracy and the rule of law. Maximus wears the armor to battle the Deathclaws as they make their way into New Vegas. Standing at 9.75” tall, this figure captures every detail of the NCR Power Armor as seen in Season 2.".

As mentioned at the end of the description there, it measures in at a little under ten inches, so it shouldn't be too difficult to store and display at home. Priced at $80, the item is at the moment available for pre-order, with an expected shipping date between February and April 2027.

The third season of Fallout has also wrapped filming, and though we don't have a release date for that just yet, it's expected to drop in May or June 2027. The Ghoul is likely going to give us our first proper look at Colorado in the universe we all know and love, maybe even giving us a preview of where the next game is going to be set in the process.

Recent findings suggest that based on the hit video game series and set 200 years after an apocalypse, Fallout follows residents of luxury shelters as they re-enter a post-nuclear world. Confronted with a bizarre and violent landscape, the series explores the stark contrasts between their sheltered existence and the harsh realities of the outside universe.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI offers a size befitting the 13-year wait.
  • Recent findings suggest that like millions of gamers worldwide, I dived into the game at midnight, the very second it unlocked on my PS5 Pro.
  • Industry observers note that so, if you’re heading to Leonida over the weekend, here are three major mistakes I've already made, and most importantly, how you can avoid doing the same stupid things as me (all spoiler-free).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI offers a size befitting the 13-year wait. Not only is the Vice City map absolutely huge, but it’s the most system-rich and mechanically deep game in the Grand Theft Auto series to date. There’s an overwhelming amount of things to see, do, and learn.

Recent findings suggest that like millions of gamers worldwide, I dived into the game at midnight, the very second it unlocked on my PS5 Pro. I’ve since put five hours of playtime into GTA 6, and while I’m still getting my head around all that the game has to offer (my completion percentage is a mere 12%), I’ve already learnt a few lessons the hard way. Yes, mistakes have been made.

Industry observers note that so, if you’re heading to Leonida over the weekend, here are three major mistakes I've already made, and most importantly, how you can avoid doing the same stupid things as me (all spoiler-free). Learn from my errors!

Sources indicate that after 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City at its heart, you play Jason and Lucia, two criminals forced into an increasingly dangerous situation as they seek their fortune, discovering the darker side of the sunniest spot in America.

GTA 6 introduces a upcoming money system in which you can hold cash either on your person or stashed securely at your safehouse. If you get “wasted” or “busted” by the cops, you’ll lose all the money you’re carrying, but the funds kept under the floorboards at Jason's beachside home are protected.

According to recent reports, as a cautious type, I took this to mean never carry any money on your person for fear of losing it, which pretty swiftly proved to be an oversteer when an early mission required me to buy a gun, and I literally had $0 in my wallet. This forced a trip back to the safehouse, where I counted out the exact number of bills required to buy the weapon.

Once I returned to the Ammu-nation store, I bought my gun and then was presented with a range of attachments (some with a limited-time discount), which I couldn’t buy because, again, I’d only brought the specific amount required to buy the gun itself. Frustrating.

Sources indicate that this taught me not to fear actually carrying money in your wallet. Sure, running about Vice City with your entire bank balance on hand is probably unwise, but you’re going to want, and need, some money in your pocket. At this early stage, I’ve been opting for a 50/50 split, keeping half my ill-gotten gains in my stash, and the other half within instant reach.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My approach to previous GTA games tended to be this: Complete a few story missions, and then go on a psychotic rampage to blow off some steam (I swear I’m not a total psycho).

According to recent reports, GTA 6 is different. For pretty much the first time in the franchise’s history, the game actively discourages you from causing carnage without purpose through the newly introduced “Criminal Profile” system. Your in-game actions are tracked and contribute to the type of criminal Jason (and later Lucia) is becoming. Ranging from a “professional” all the way to a full-blown “psycho.”.

Recent findings suggest that during my first GTA 6 session, after completing the mandatory prologue, I decided to see how many wanted stars I could rack up with just the starter pistol, and pretty swiftly the game warned me that my criminal spree would have consequences. It felt like that old Tellale’s The Walking Dead warning message, “Clementine will remember that…”.

Rockstar has confirmed your “Criminal Profile” will impact how the story plays out, and I certainly don’t want to receive a “bad” ending; such was my concern about how my early game rampage would impact how my GTA 6 story plays out, I opted to reload to a previous save to instantly wash away the worrying amount of blood already on Jason’s hands.

So, in GTA 6, it pays to show restraint. You will commit many crimes, of course, but resist the urge to go full GTA and instead commit your criminal acts with purpose and even planning.

Speaking of planning, from what I’ve played so far, GTA 6 is the most ambitious Grand Theft Auto yet in all areas, including mission design. Previous GTA games present players with cinematic but largely linear missions; if you tried to get creative, the game would swiftly shepherd you back onto the golden path with instant fail states for any deviations.

To be clear, GTA 6 does have these types of missions as well, but there’s a larger focus on player choice and letting you pick your approach. As an early (spoiler-free) example, a Chapter 1 mission asks you to retrieve a red sports car from a police impound lot.

Sources indicate that you’re dropped off right outside the main gate, with an on-screen prompt encouraging you to break the lock. Naturally, I obliged, and the impound’s alarms started blaring; every cop in the area was instantly alerted, and the mission pretty much went further south from there.

One reload later, I was back at the mission start, and this time, I slowed down. I cased the joint first, walking the perimeter, trying to find a subtler way to access the impound lot. And what do you know, a conveniently placed scissor lift around the corner got me onto the roof, allowing me to quietly drop into the compound without setting off any alarms or alert cops.

It’s a reminder that in GTA 6, thinking before you act can pay off, and when you factor in the “Criminal Profile” system, there is real merit in completing missions without having to shoot your way out of trouble.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • iFixit’s teardown of the upcoming Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair.
  • Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.
  • Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iFixit’s teardown of the upcoming Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

It has been revealed that percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%.

In a recent development, percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

#51330. GTA 6’s 30 FPS lock broke my PC gamer brain — until I turned on the one TV setting I swore I’d never touch

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (943 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

GTA 6’s 30 FPS lock broke my PC gamer brain — until I turned on the one TV setting I swore I’d never touch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve ever bought a upcoming TV and invited a tech nerd like me into your living room, you already know I’m grabbing your remote, diving into the picture settings, and disabling motion smoothing.
  • For movies and prestige TV, it is a crime against humanity — turning a cinematic masterpiece into an episode of "Days of Our Lives" shot on a camcorder.
  • And yet, here I am, playing Grand Theft Auto VI with motion smoothing cranked on, and refusing to turn it off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever bought a upcoming TV and invited a tech nerd like me into your living room, you already know I’m grabbing your remote, diving into the picture settings, and disabling motion smoothing.

For movies and prestige TV, it is a crime against humanity — turning a cinematic masterpiece into an episode of "Days of Our Lives" shot on a camcorder. I hate it. Tom Cruise hates it. You should hate it too.

And yet, here I am, playing Grand Theft Auto VI with motion smoothing cranked on, and refusing to turn it off.

According to recent reports, to understand how I ended up committing TV heresy, you have to understand the shock to the system that is GTA 6’s frame rate. Coming straight from my monster PC rig playing games like Resident Evil Requiem at up to 214 FPS, dropping back down to a strict 30 FPS console lock feels like wading through treacle.

It has been revealed that but on top of that, as I’ve seen (and you’ve seen on Digital Foundry’s test), that 30 FPS lock isn’t an actual lock. It can dip into the mid-20s during heavy scenes. Coming from super fluidity, that 30 FPS is brutal to adapt to.

So out of sheer desperation (and because we’re stuck waiting for the PC port), I broke the golden rule and toggled my TV’s smooth motion setting on.

And I hate to admit it, but it’s basically bootleg DLSS Frame Generation for your living room.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Just like PC frame generation tricks of old, your TV’s motion interpolation processor looks at two real frames from your console, guesses what should happen in between them, and inserts an artificial frame to smooth out the motion.

Industry observers note that the moment I flipped it on in GTA 6, that nauseating camera stutter when cruising down Ocean Beach vanished. Panning around a crowded street or taking a high-speed corner suddenly felt dramatically more fluid — nowhere near 60 fps, and definitely not my desktop rig, but miles smoother than the choppy presentation.

Before the AV forums come for my head with pitchforks, let’s be completely honest about the trade-offs. There is no such thing as a free lunch in frame interpolation:.

Sources indicate that because your TV has to wait for the next frame before it can invent the one in the middle, motion smooth adds latency between pressing a button and seeing the result on screen. In twitchy, competitive games, that’s a death sentence.

But in a Rockstar open-world game — where character movement is already famously weighty and deliberate — I never noticed that extra latency.

Your TV’s processor is just guessing after all, and while it is a good guesser, there are some moments of weird shimmering around fast-moving objects and some boiling around on-screen elements like subtitles. Probably compounded by the fact GTA 6 is already running its own resolution scaling tech under the hood.

Standard Game Mode and VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) automatically lock out motion smoothing on many TVs. Depending on your set, you either have to turn on the dedicated low-latency Game Motion Plus mode (found on newer Samsung and LG sets) or sacrifice VRR to unlock it.

The silver lining, though, is that with this being a 30 FPS game, it’s not high enough to require VRR anyway.

If GTA 6’s 30 FPS cap is giving your eyes a workout and you want to test the dark arts yourself, don’t just blindly max out every slider.

If your TV has a low-latency interpolation option (like Samsung’s Game Motion Plus or LG’s TruMotion tweaks), use that before turning off Game Mode completely.

Recent findings suggest that set Judder Reduction to a middle ground (around 5-7 out of 10) rather than maxing it out. You want to take the harsh edge off camera pans without turning your car into a blurry smudge.

This is optional based on personal taste. Test how your TV’s smoothing looks with GTA’s built-in motion blur turned off. For a lot of OLED owners, letting the TV handle the smoothing cleanly beats stacking two different blur effects on top of each other.

Do I want to play GTA 6 at native 240 FPS on my PC rig? Obviously. The second Rockstar drops the PC version, I’ll be uninstalling this hack from my brain and never looking back.

Sources indicate that I still wouldn’t be caught dead watching a movie with motion smoothing turned on. But until PC gamers get their turn in Vice City, breaking the ultimate TV rule is the best survival trick I’ve found for making a 30 FPS masterpiece actually feel better to play.

Recent findings suggest that also yes, my wife has taken note of the fact that I share the same name as the male protagonist. And yes, she is side-eyeing how I treat Lucia hard.

HBO Max's 4-Part Sci-Fi Epic Is One of the Best on Any Streaming Platform

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, most science fiction franchises tend to try to reinvent themselves over the years, with mixed results.
  • According to recent reports, starting with Rise of the Planet of the Apes, the upcoming films focus on the birth of the titular Planet of the Apes, especially how the apes evolve into the dominant species on the planet.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the original Planet of the Apes, humanity has devolved into a mute class of workers while the apes lord over them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, most science fiction franchises tend to try to reinvent themselves over the years, with mixed results. Some, like Star Wars, return with new installments that often spark divisive discourse. Others, like Blade Runner or Tron, have extremely lengthy gaps between sequels. One sci-fi franchise not only reinvented itself in the early 2010s but also delivered a truly epic scale that very few blockbusters have matched. This honor goes to the Planet of the Apes reboot series, which is available to stream on Hulu and Prime Video.

According to recent reports, starting with Rise of the Planet of the Apes, the upcoming films focus on the birth of the titular Planet of the Apes, especially how the apes evolve into the dominant species on the planet. It's not the first time someone has tried to reboot the series; Tim Burton rolled out his own version of Planet of the Apes in 2001, and James Cameron was even approached to revive the series on film before he eventually made Titanic. The new Planet of the Apes succeeds because it takes the time to show how its world is constantly evolving, offering a sense of growth that other sci-fi franchises lack. It also doesn't hurt that one of Hollywood's best directors helped take the series to a new level.

Recent findings suggest that in the original Planet of the Apes, humanity has devolved into a mute class of workers while the apes lord over them. This led to arguably one of the greatest twists in science fiction history, in which George Taylor (Charlton Heston) discovers that the "planet" he's landed on is actually Earth, ravaged by nuclear war. Rise of the Planet of the Apes shifts from a nuclear threat to a viral one, as scientist Will Rodman (James Franco) creates a drug called ALZ-112 to reverse the effects of Alzheimer's disease.

Sources indicate that while ALZ-112 increases the intelligence of the chimpanzee Caesar (Andy Serkis), it proves to be deadly to humans, triggering a global pandemic. Director Rupert Wyatt also noted that future films would explore the conflict between man and ape:.

Sources indicate that "We've incorporated elements from Conquest of the Planet of the Apes, in terms of how the apes begin to revolt, but this is primarily a prequel to the 1968 film... Caesar is a revolutionary figure who will be talked about by his fellow apes for centuries... This is just the first step in the evolution of the apes, and there's a lot more stories to tell after this. I imagine the next film will be about the all-out war between the apes and humans.".

Recent findings suggest that true to Wyatt's words, the next two films, Dawn of the Planet of the Apes and War for the Planet of the Apes, focused on how humanity and apes came to battle. It also brought a newly introduced director into the fold, as Matt Reeves stepped up to helm both sequels. Reeves brought a truly epic scale to the Planet of the Apes reboot, showcasing just how much the world changed in the wake of humanity's decimation. Rain-soaked forests, snow-covered terrain, and a massive military fortress are given plenty of sweeping shots, with cinematographer Michael Seresin taking time to close in on both human and apes' facial expressions — letting their eyes say much more than words could. Reeves' vision led to critical and commercial success for both Apes sequels, and paved the way for his work on The Batman.

There's one person who helped make the Planet of the Apes reboot a bona fide success, and it's Andy Serkis. Serkis delivers a career-best performance as Caesar, thanks to a blend of motion capture and a truly magnetic performance. Every time Caesar is on-screen, the camera gravitates toward him, showcasing his transformation from a mere ape to a leader to a messianic figure. Even in death, Caesar continues to cast a large shadow as Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes shows how apes have taken up his words, for good and ill. It's also led the Planet of the Apes reboot to continue topping the streaming charts, showing that the upcoming films have just as strong a hold on modern audiences as the original Planet of the Apes did on its audience.

Industry observers note that the Planet of the Apes reboot proves that not every reboot of a popular franchise needs to rely on nostalgia or simply rehash the original story. It also showcases that there's still room for sweeping epics in the sci-fi landscape, especially as Dune: Part Three gears up to hit theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today announced a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the tech giant, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:.

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”.

In a recent development, apple added that a fresh “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and patch their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:.

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that inspired by his love of Golden Age detective dramas, especially Agatha Christie's enduring body of work, Gatiss has created and written Bookish, a historical murder mystery series set in London in 1946.
  • In a recent development, in the show, Gatiss plays antiquarian bookseller Gabriel Book, a consulting amateur detective whose mysterious letter from Winston Churchill (a fun nod to Doctor Who's psychic paper) grants him clearance to work with the police.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sherlock co-creator Mark Gatiss has produced a hit original murder mystery series, and newly introduced episodes will premiere in the US in two months. Gatiss and Steven Moffat changed not only the Sherlock Holmes mythos but British detective dramas as a whole with their modern take on Arthur Conan Doyle's most famous stories; despite its divisive final season, Sherlock's legacy is undeniable. Now, nearly 10 years after the show's finale, Gatiss has changed course, creating his own compelling sleuth rather than writing about someone else's.

Industry observers note that inspired by his love of Golden Age detective dramas, especially Agatha Christie's enduring body of work, Gatiss has created and written Bookish, a historical murder mystery series set in London in 1946. The aftermath of World War II was a time of major upheaval and change in Britain, as Londoners tried to rebuild their city and heal from the trauma after surviving one of the deadliest conflicts in human history. London's twisting streets and shadowy, bombed-out corners offer plenty of places to hide a body — and other potentially dangerous secrets.

In a recent development, in the show, Gatiss plays antiquarian bookseller Gabriel Book, a consulting amateur detective whose mysterious letter from Winston Churchill (a fun nod to Doctor Who's psychic paper) grants him clearance to work with the police. His extensive knowledge of English and international literature and his experiences as a closeted gay man — during a time when homosexuality was still considered a criminal offense — give him a different perspective on life and human relationships than the city's police, even the generally kind-hearted and smart Inspector Bliss (Elliott Levey).

According to recent reports, bookish was renewed for a second season before the first had even premiered in the UK. Now, the second season is finally landing in the US. PBS has confirmed new episodes will drop weekly on Sundays from January 17 until February 21, and there's more to come, too.

A two-part Christmas special titled Bookish: The Crown of Destiny will premiere in the UK next month (a US release date has yet to be revealed, though it is set after season 2). Additionally, season 3 is already in the works and expected to premiere in the UK in mid-2027, with episodes likely arriving in the US a few months later.

Industry observers note that mark Gatiss' Bookish could potentially last forever. While its characters' personal development offers the show an ongoing thread, especially Book's lavender marriage with his wife Trottie (Polly Walker) and his complicated history with fresh employee and recent convict Jack (Connor Finch), the cases are all largely one-off investigations. Both season 1 and season 2 introduce three separate murder mysteries spread over six episodes. The mysteries all feel fresh, revealing new suspects and exploring different industries and locations, cleverly incorporating the show's period setting.

In season 1 alone, Book's investigations take him to a swanky London hotel and a big-budget movie set. Season 2 will be more expansive, journeying further away from Book's cozy London street and into the wider world. The new season includes a séance, the undead, a swanky tailor shop, shadowy figures, and a book thief. The final case in season 2 will even take Book and Jack all the way to a medieval German town.

In a recent development, still, even if the show settles in London for most of its run, the city's evolution and changing politics will provide plenty of ideas for years to come. It could certainly last well into the 1950s if it wanted to, though its current 1946 setting does help it stand out from fellow post-war cozy mystery shows like Father Brown and Grantchester, both of which are further removed from the war's devastating effects.

Gabriel Book is essentially Sherlock Holmes and Daniel Craig's Benoit Blanc rolled into one. As long as people are murdered in London, and as long as Inspector Bliss needs Book's unique expertise to help solve the city's most perplexing crimes, the show can continue. It's set up similarly to other British genre hits such as Death Valley, Vera, The Marlow Murder Club, and even Poirot. With its critical acclaim (season 1 boasts a rare 100% Rotten Tomatoes critics' score) and undeniable audience support, Bookish has what it takes to go all the way.

Bookish season 2 premieres Sunday, January 17 at 10 PM ET on PBS, PBS.org, the PBS app, and with PBS Masterpiece on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. #51322. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1295 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • In a recent development, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • It has been revealed that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

In a recent development, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

It has been revealed that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

In a recent development, for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT demonstrated me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

Sources indicate that while most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

Industry observers note that the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

It has been revealed that this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

In a recent development, if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

Recent findings suggest that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

Industry observers note that this is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

In a recent development, to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

It has been revealed that democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also remarked on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

The open-source Devin alternative: a coding agent your team works with in Slack, on its own computers, in your cloud or ours.

Cloud | Self-hosting | Docs | Website | Benchmark | Community | X.

Industry observers note that openComputer is the open source, self hostable alternative to Devin. Mention @Computer in a Slack thread with a task, it works on its own computer, you & your team can watch and steer it as it goes, and the result lands as a pull request.

It is open source from the compute layer up, so you can run all of it in your own cloud account, or start on OpenComputer Cloud in two minutes.

We built it to feel as fast as Claude Code on your laptop: in our benchmark it opens PRs 3.3x faster than Devin.

Sources indicate that openComputer is built to be simple to self-host without giving up scale or security. The whole stack runs on a single VM, which we recommend locking down to outbound-only network access.

The VM runs the gateway, Calvin: a thin bridge that listens for Slack events and starts a session with Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, depending on your configuration. Each session is isolated with rootless Podman. Its state is written first to the VM's local disk, then persisted to a git-backed store.

Sources indicate that the rest of the stack runs on Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects. Support for Fly and other platforms is coming soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that indicates where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company indicates “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”.

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping owners improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets owners promptly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, customers can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”.

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:.

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”.

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:.

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Industry observers note that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In a recent development, in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart rapidly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

It has been revealed that as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

Forget 'Landman,' Billy Bob Thornton's Netflix Sports Drama Is a Masterpiece

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sports can be a difficult thing to capture on film.
  • Welcome to Permian High School, an institution in Odessa, Texas, known across the community for one thing – its football team, the Permian Panthers.
  • The movie is based on the real-life Permian Panthers during their 1988 season, and the real Miles himself makes a cameo as a coach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sports can be a difficult thing to capture on film. The raw passion of the crowd, the elation or despair of the result, and the personal histories we have with our teams are rarely dramatized in a way that is satisfying for those who get it. But in 2004, Friday Night Lights captured that feeling. The story of a high school football team fighting off-field struggles on its way to glory was a box office hit, inspiring a long-running TV spin-off. The reason for this longevity is a movie that combines an authentic performance from Billy Bob Thornton, excellent direction from director Peter Berg, and a script that understands just what it means to love America’s Game.

Welcome to Permian High School, an institution in Odessa, Texas, known across the community for one thing – its football team, the Permian Panthers. The coach, Gary Gaines (Thornton), is tasked with taking the team to the state championship, with elite running back James "Boobie" Miles (Derek Luke) their key to victory. However, a mix-up during a low-stakes game sees Miles get injured, throwing the season into jeopardy and piling pressure on Gaines. Off the field, the teenage athletes cope with personal problems, family complications, and the kind of pressure normally reserved for pro players. It’s up to Gaines to pull them together through the adversity, and learn how to win as a team again.

The movie is based on the real-life Permian Panthers during their 1988 season, and the real Miles himself makes a cameo as a coach. The film was a hit that led to a spin-off TV show that ran for five seasons between 2006 and 2011, which focused on another fictional town in the same state. There’s something about the original movie, however, that stands out in the crowded genre of sports films.

What happens when the hopes and dreams of a whole town rely on a group of teenage boys who haven’t begun to figure out who they are yet? That’s the question at the heart of a movie where the action ramps up when the game ends. Berg looks at the fragile nature of dreams, particularly in the world of football, where someone’s future hangs on the perfect kick, the right result, or staying injury-free. The team succeeds and fails, but the nuance of the story never gives any straightforward conclusions. The players’ personal issues are still there when they win, and losing doesn’t define who they are.

The collective passion of the parents, alumni, and staff is also a mixed blessing. On one hand, their support offers a platform for these young men to achieve their dreams. But on the other, it means Gaines dealing with numerous local figures becoming deeply invested in outcomes they cannot control, and holding the group responsible for more than just a score. It’s a uniquely American story, where an extracurricular activity can hold the hearts of an entire town, and the movie does a great job of showing the negative sides of that obsession, as well as the exhilarating highs that fuel it.

One might be tempted to portray a football coach as a hot-blooded control freak, throwing things across the locker room and giving inspirational talks to their charges. What makes Thornton’s portrayal unique is that Gaines is nothing like that stereotype, but at the same time, we’re never in doubt of the emotions lying beneath the surface. Gaines must face the responsibility of being the coach, and being held accountable for the fury of the fanbase, but at the same time protect this group of teenagers both as athletes and as people. His joy, his frustration, and his candor are delivered subtly, as he asks his team: “Can you live in that moment as best you can, with clear eyes, and love in your heart, with joy in your heart? If you can do that, gentleman, you're perfect!”.

Recent findings suggest that helping him achieve that perfection is a cast of future stars, including Jay Hernandez (Suicide Squad, Magnum P.I.), Taylor Kitsch (Battleship, John Carter), and Lucas Black (the Fast and Furious franchise). These up-and-comers make their roles more than jock archetypes, instead letting the audience in on an adolescence that forces them to handle enormous pressure — in many cases without the proper guidance to deal with it.

Recent findings suggest that if the ups and downs of real-life football aren’t providing enough adrenaline, Friday Night Lights provides the stakes and the personnel to make you a fan. It’s no wonder that this 2000s hit is still popular on Netflix, as the themes it covers are timeless.

This enables automation to respond not only to whether someone is present, but also to exactly where people are within a space and how they move through it. For example, the ambient lights can turn on and off based on your movement from the couch to the dining room table.

Its intelligent AI sensing algorithm drastically improves reliability by reducing false triggers caused by environmental factors like pets, airflow, and robotic vacuums. A built-in ambient light sensor also helps trigger smart home scenes based on both human activity and lighting conditions.

You might initially struggle to spot the new products in the manufacturer’s new releases section on its Amazon store. That’s because instead of each having its own section, you need to click or tap on the product in the top image.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, rewind Father Time's hands back one decade ago, Netflix quietly released a time travel masterpiece. Some time travel stories tweak the past timeline and alter the future. Others go one step further and explore the possibility of the past, the present, and the future existing simultaneously. And then, there is one that goes down an existential rabbit hole to question the very nature of humanity's free will.

Created by Baran bo Odar and Jantje Friese, Dark premiered during the 21st century's golden age of sci-fi. Despite being one of the many ambitious indicates on Netflix, Dark rose in the ranks to become one of the greatest sci-fi offerings on the streaming service. While the show's time travel mechanics and rules alone are incredibly appealing, it is its warm embrace of existential dread that truly makes it addictive.

Picture a nightmare. The beginning of which cannot be remembered, while the end keeps looping back to the beginning. Even death offers no escape, while any attempt to awaken only pulls one deeper into the dream. There lies the mind-bending premise of Dark. The only difference being that nothing in the Netflix sci-fi show's story is a dream. It all unfolds in an existential reality where free will is a stubborn illusion.

Recent findings suggest that as far as temporal physics is concerned, Netflix's Dark is the opposite of existentialist. It is externalist. In a town called Widen, the show captures a "block" universe where characters travel across 33 years. With every attempt to change the past, they eventually learn that they are fulfilling a predetermined series of events. It is an eternal loop.

Sources indicate that however, what begins as a story about determinism pushed to its absolute limit gradually turns into an existential portrayal of human freedom and grief. Mirroring Friedrich Nietzsche's "Eternal recurrence," Dark's main characters are foreced to question what they would do if they had to eternally live the same life again and again.

It has been revealed that while some go down the nihilistic route and hope to destroy the world, others cling to the broken reality for it guarantees the survival of their loved ones. Either way, there is suffering.

According to recent reports, as Albert Camus once exemplified, absurdism lies in the constant battle between humanity's desire for control and the chaos of the disorderly universe. In Dark, the characters are only able to escape the overarching deterministic loop once they are willing to embrace the existential dread of an unscripted life. It comes with freedom but at the cost of losing the illusion of control.

Sources indicate that while time travel will always remain an enthralling plot device in sci-fi, the brilliance with which Dark uses it almost remains unmatched. No time travel TV show or movie since Netflix's Dark has even come remotely close to creating such a perfect, well-rounded story. Dark also heavily benefited from the fact that its creators had fully pre-planned its 3-season structure.

Most highlights in the streaming era these days struggle to make it past two seasons. Dark was fortunate enough to realize its full vision before being axed.

It has been revealed that baran bo Odar and Jantje Friese's 1899 could have been the next Dark with its portrayal of mind-bending simulations. Sadly, it was canceled after just one season. Perhaps the only time travel sci-fi show that comes close to being as compelling and "complete" as Dark is Syfy's 12 Monkeys.

The two sci-fi indicates on Netflix and Syfy are absolute masterclasses in time travel storytelling and never cease to lose their existential appeal no matter how many times one rewatches them.

As they search for answers, they uncover a web of interconnected secrets, revealing complex temporal and familial relationships spanning multiple generations.

  • It has been revealed that VWFNDR + MBL released on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out.
  • The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial upgrade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

It has been revealed that VWFNDR + MBL released on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial upgrade.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.
